3.2  Background on Risk-averse MDPs

The MDP below includes a sink state, which is different from the MDP defined in Chapter 2. Once an agent reaches the sink state, it will remain in that state and receive a reward of zero.

Markov Decision Processes

We focus on solving Markov decision processes (MDPs) [106], modeled by a tuple (𝒮¯,𝒜,p¯,r¯,𝝁¯)(\bar{\mathcal{S}},\mathcal{A},\bar{p},\bar{r},\bm{\bar{\mu}}), where 𝒮¯={1,2,…,S,S+1}\bar{\mathcal{S}}=\{1,2,\dots,S,S+1\} is the finite set of states and 𝒜={1,2,…,A}\mathcal{A}=\{1,2,\ldots,A\} is the finite set of actions. The transition function p¯:𝒮¯×𝒜→Δ𝒮¯\bar{p}\colon\bar{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{S}}} represents the probability p¯​(s,a,s′)\bar{p}(s,a,s^{\prime}) of transitioning to s′∈𝒮¯s^{\prime}\in\bar{\mathcal{S}} after taking a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} in s∈𝒮¯s\in\bar{\mathcal{S}} and 𝒑¯s​a∈Δ𝒮¯\bm{\bar{p}}_{sa}\in\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{S}}} is such that (𝒑¯s​a)s′=p¯​(s,a,s′)(\bm{\bar{p}}_{sa})_{s^{\prime}}=\bar{p}(s,a,s^{\prime}). The function r¯:𝒮¯×𝒜×𝒮¯→ℝ\bar{r}\colon\bar{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\times\bar{\mathcal{S}}\to\mathbb{R} represents the reward r¯​(s,a,s′)∈ℝ\bar{r}(s,a,s^{\prime})\in\mathbb{R} associated with transitioning from s∈𝒮¯s\in\bar{\mathcal{S}} and a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} to s′∈𝒮¯s^{\prime}\in\bar{\mathcal{S}}. The vector 𝝁¯∈Δ𝒮¯\bm{\bar{\mu}}\in\Delta_{\bar{\mathcal{S}}} is the initial state distribution.

We designate the state e:=S+1e:=S+1 as a sink state and use 𝒮={1,…,S}\mathcal{S}=\left\{1,\dots,S\right\} to denote the set of all non-sink states. The sink state ee must satisfy that p¯​(e,a,e)=1\bar{p}(e,a,e)=1 and r¯​(e,a,e)=0\bar{r}(e,a,e)=0 for each a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, and μ¯e=0\bar{\mu}_{e}=0. Throughout the paper, we use a bar to indicate whether the quantity involves the sink state ee. Note that the sink state can indicate a goal when all rewards are negative and an undesirable terminal state when all rewards are positive.

The following technical assumption is needed to simplify the derivation.

Assumption 3.2.1.

The initial distribution 𝝁\bm{\mu} satisfies that

𝝁>𝟎.\bm{\mu}>\bm{0}.

To lift Assumption 3.2.1, one needs to carefully account for infinite values, which adds complexity to the results and distracts from the main ideas.

The solution to an MDP is a policy. Given a horizon t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}, a history-dependent policy in the set ΠHRt\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}}^{t} maps the history of states and actions to a distribution over actions. A Markov policy π∈ΠMRt\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{MR}}^{t} is a sequence of decision rules π=(𝒅0,𝒅1,…,𝒅t−1)\pi=(\bm{d}_{0},\bm{d}_{1},\dots,\bm{d}_{t-1}) with 𝒅k:𝒮→Δ𝒜\bm{d}_{k}\colon\mathcal{S}\to\Delta_{\mathcal{A}} the decision rule for taking actions at time kk. The set of all randomized decision rules is 𝒟=(Δ𝒜)𝒮\mathcal{D}=(\Delta_{\mathcal{A}})^{\mathcal{S}}. Stationary policies ΠSR\Pi_{\mathrm{SR}} are Markov policies with π:=(𝒅)∞:=(𝒅,𝒅,…)\pi:=(\bm{d})_{\infty}:=(\bm{d},\bm{d},\dots) with the identical decision rule in every timestep. We treat decision rules and stationary policies interchangeably. The sets of deterministic Markov and stationary policies are denoted by ΠMDt\Pi_{\mathrm{MD}}^{t} and ΠSD\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}}. Finally, we omit the superscript tt to indicate infinite horizon definitions of policies.

The risk-neutral Total Reward Criterion (TRC) objective is:

supπ∈ΠHRlim inft→∞𝔼π,𝝁​[∑k=0t−1r⁡(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)],\sup_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}}}\liminf_{t\to\infty}\mathbb{E}^{\pi,\bm{\mu}}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right], (3.1)

where the random variables are denoted by a tilde and s~k\tilde{s}_{k} and a~k\tilde{a}_{k} represent the state from 𝒮¯\bar{\mathcal{S}} and action at time kk. The superscript π\pi denotes the policy that governs the actions a~k\tilde{a}_{k} when visiting s~k\tilde{s}_{k}, and 𝝁\bm{\mu} denotes the initial distribution. Finally, note that lim inf\liminf gives a conservative estimate of a policy’s return since the limit does not necessarily exist for non-stationary policies.

Unlike the discounted criterion, the risk-neutral TRC may be unbounded, optimal policies may not exist, or may be non-stationary [65, 109]. To circumvent these issues, we assume that all policies have a positive probability of eventually transitioning to the sink state.

Assumption 3.2.2.

The MDP is transient. That is, for each π∈ΠSD\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}}:

∑t=0∞ℙπ,s[s~t=s′]<∞,∀s,s′∈𝒮.\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}^{\pi,s}\left[\tilde{s}_{t}=s^{\prime}\right]\;<\;\infty,\qquad\forall s,s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}. (3.2)

Assumption 3.2.2 underlies most of our results. Transient MDPs are important because their optimal policies exist and can be chosen to be stationary deterministic (4, theorem 4.12). Transient MDPs are also common in stochastic games [107] and generalize the stochastic shortest path problem [65].

An important tool in their analysis is the spectral radius ρ:ℝn×n→ℝ\rho\colon\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\to\mathbb{R} which is defined for each 𝑨∈ℝn×n\bm{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} as the maximum absolute eigenvalue: ρ⁡(𝑨):=maxi=1,…,n⁡|λi|\rho(\bm{A}):=\max_{i=1,\dots,n}|\lambda_{i}| where λi\lambda_{i} is the ii-th eigenvalue [110].

Lemma 3.2.3 (Theorem 4.8 in [4]).

An MDP is transient if and only if ρ⁡(𝐏π)<1\rho(\bm{P}^{\pi})<1 for all π∈ΠSR\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SR}}.

Now, we discuss the differences between a discounted MDP and a transient MDP, which are useful in demonstrating the behavior of risk-averse objectives. The discounted infinite-horizon ERM objective for a discount factor γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1), a policy π∈ΠSD\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}}, and β>0\beta>0 is

ργ​(π,β):=ERMπ,𝝁⁡[∑t=0∞γt⋅r⁡(s~t,a~t,s~t+1)].\rho_{\gamma}(\pi,\beta):=\ermo^{\pi,\bm{\mu}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\cdot r(\tilde{s}_{t},\tilde{a}_{t},\tilde{s}_{t+1})\right]. (3.3)

In the risk-neutral setting, it is well-known that the discounted objective can be interpreted as TRC (111, Section 1.10). That is, every discounted MDP can be converted to a transient MDP. Given an MDP ℳ=(𝒮,𝒜,p,r,μ)\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},p,r,\mu), we construct a transient MDP ℳ¯γ=(𝒮¯,𝒜,p¯,r¯,μ¯)\bar{\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma}=(\bar{\mathcal{S}},\mathcal{A},\bar{p},\bar{r},\bar{\mu}) such that 𝒮¯=𝒮∪{e}\bar{\mathcal{S}}=\mathcal{S}\cup\left\{e\right\}, and μ¯​(s)=μ⁡(s),∀s∈𝒮\bar{\mu}(s)=\mu(s),\forall s\in\mathcal{S} and μ⁡(e)=0\mu(e)=0. The transition function p¯\bar{p} is defined as

p¯​(s,a,s′)={γ⋅p⁡(s,a,s′)ifs,s′∈𝒮,a∈𝒜,1−γifs∈𝒮,s′=e,a∈𝒜,1ifs=s′=e,a∈𝒜,0otherwise.\bar{p}(s,a,s^{\prime})\;=\;\begin{cases}\gamma\cdot p(s,a,s^{\prime})\quad&\text{if}\quad s,s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A},\\ 1-\gamma\quad&\text{if}\quad s\in\mathcal{S},s^{\prime}=e,a\in\mathcal{A},\\ 1\quad&\text{if}\quad s=s^{\prime}=e,a\in\mathcal{A},\\ 0\quad&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (3.4)

When the rewards r:𝒮×𝒜→ℝr\colon\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R} are independent of the next state, then r¯:𝒮¯×𝒜→ℝ\bar{r}\colon\bar{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R} are defined as

r¯​(s,a)={r⁡(s,a)if ​s∈𝒮,0otherwise.\bar{r}(s,a)=\begin{cases}r(s,a)&\text{if }s\in\mathcal{S},\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (3.5)

The model can be readily extended to account for the target state dependence by constructing an ℳ¯γ\bar{\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma} with the reward function r¯:𝒮¯×𝒜×𝒮¯→ℝ\bar{r}\colon\bar{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\times\bar{\mathcal{S}}\to\mathbb{R} as

r¯​(s,a,s′)={γ−1⋅r⁡(s,a,s′)if ​s,s′∈𝒮,0otherwise.\bar{r}(s,a,s^{\prime})=\begin{cases}\gamma^{-1}\cdot r(s,a,s^{\prime})&\text{if }s,s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S},\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Recall that when β=0\beta=0, we have limβ→0+ERM⁡[x~]=𝔼⁡[x~]\lim_{\beta\rightarrow 0^{+}}\ermo[\tilde{x}]=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{x}].

Proposition 3.2.4 shows that the expected total returns are identical in a discounted MDP ℳ\mathcal{M} and in a transient MDP ℳ¯γ\bar{\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma}.

Proposition 3.2.4.

For each γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1) and MDPs ℳ,ℳ¯γ\mathcal{M},\bar{\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma} constructed in Section 3.2, we have that

ργ​(π,0)=g∞​(π,0),π∈ΠSD.\rho_{\gamma}(\pi,0)\;=\;g_{\infty}(\pi,0),\quad\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}}.

where ργ​(π,0)\rho_{\gamma}(\pi,0) is defined in (3.3) and g∞​(π,0)g_{\infty}(\pi,0) is defined in (3.9).

Proof.

The proposition follows from the construction above by algebraic manipulation (111, section 1.10). ∎

Consider an example in Figure 3.1. There is one non-sink state ss and one action aa. A triple tuple represents an action, a transition probability, and a reward separately. For the discounted MDP, the discount factor is γ\gamma. For the transient MDP, ee is the sink state, and there is a positive probability 1−ϵ1-\epsilon that it will transit from state ss to state ee. Once the agent reaches the state ee, it stays in ee.

Monetary risk measures

Monetary risk measures aim to generalize the expectation operator to account for the spread of the random variable. Entropic risk measure (ERM) is a popular risk measure, defined for any risk level β>0\beta>0 and x~∈𝕏\tilde{x}\in\mathbb{X} as [78]

ERMβ[x~]=−β−1⋅log𝔼exp(−β⋅x~).\displaystyle\ermo_{\beta}\left[\tilde{x}\right]\;=\;-\beta^{-1}\cdot\log\mathbb{E}\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot\tilde{x}\right). (3.6)

and extended to β∈[0,∞]\beta\in[0,\infty] as ERM0⁡[x~]=limβ→0+ERMβ⁡[x~]=𝔼⁡[x~]\ermo_{0}[\tilde{x}]=\lim_{\beta\to 0^{+}}\ermo_{\beta}\left[\tilde{x}\right]=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{x}] and ERM∞[x~]=limβ→∞ERMβ[x~]=essinf[x~]\ermo_{\infty}[\tilde{x}]=\lim_{\beta\to\infty}\ermo_{\beta}\left[\tilde{x}\right]=\operatorname{ess}\inf[\tilde{x}]. ERM plays a unique role in sequential decision-making because it is the only law-invariant risk measure that satisfies the tower property shown in Proposition 3.2.5, which is essential in constructing dynamic programs [39]. Unfortunately, two significant limitations of ERM hinder its practical applications. First, ERM is not positively homogenous and, therefore, the risk value depends on the scale of the rewards, and ERM is not coherent [78, 39, 48]. Second, the risk parameter β\beta is challenging to interpret and does not relate well to other standard risk measures, like VaR or CVaR.

For these reasons, we focus on the Entropic Value at Risk (EVaR), defined as, for a given α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1),

EVaRα⁡[x~]\displaystyle\evaro_{\alpha}\left[\tilde{x}\right] =supβ>0−β−1log(α−1𝔼exp(−βx~))\displaystyle=\;\sup_{\beta>0}-\beta^{-1}\log\left(\alpha^{-1}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\tilde{x}\right)\right) (3.7)
=supβ>0ERMβ⁡[x~]+β−1​log⁡α,\displaystyle=\;\sup_{\beta>0}\ermo_{\beta}\left[\tilde{x}\right]+\beta^{-1}\log\alpha,

and extended to EVaR0[x~]=essinf[x~]\evaro_{0}\left[\tilde{x}\right]=\ess\inf[\tilde{x}] and EVaR1⁡[x~]=𝔼⁡[x~]\evaro_{1}\left[\tilde{x}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\tilde{x}\right] [48]. It is important to note that the supremum in (4.2) may not be attained even when x~\tilde{x} is a finite discrete random variable [49].

EVaR addresses the limitations of ERM while preserving its benefits. EVaR is coherent and positively homogenous. EVaR is also a good approximation to interpretable quantile-based risk measures, like VaR and CVaR [48, 39].

Proposition 3.2.5.

Tower Property for ERM (39, theorem 3.1)

For any two random variables x~1,x~2∈𝕏\tilde{x}_{1},\tilde{x}_{2}\in\mathbb{X}, we have

ERMβ⁡[x~1]=ERMβ⁡[ERMβ⁡[x~1∣x~2]],\ermo_{\beta}[\tilde{x}_{1}]=\ermo_{\beta}[\ermo_{\beta}[\tilde{x}_{1}\mid\tilde{x}_{2}]],

where the conditional ERM is defined as

ERMβ⁡[x~1|x~2]=−β−1​log⁡(𝔼⁡[e−β​x~1∣x~2])\ermo_{\beta}[\tilde{x}_{1}|\tilde{x}_{2}]=-\beta^{-1}\log(\mathbb{E}[e^{-\beta\tilde{x}_{1}}\mid\tilde{x}_{2}])
Risk-averse MDPs.

Risk-averse MDPs, using static VaR and CVaR risk measures, under the discounted criterion received abundant attention [54, 43, 44, 45, 46], showing that these objectives require history-dependent optimal policies. In contrast, nested risk measures under the TRC may admit stationary policies that can be computed using dynamic programming [63, 31, 60, 66]. However, the TRC with nested CVaR can be unbounded, as shown in Proposition 3.2.6. Recent work has shown that optimal Markov policies exist for EVaR discounted objectives, and they can be computed via dynamic programming [39], building upon similar results established for ERM [112]. However, in TRC with ERM, the value functions may also be unbounded (67, proposition D.1).

The following proposition contradicts (63, theorem 1).

Proposition 3.2.6.

There exists a transient MDP and a risk level α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) such that the TRC with nested CVaR or EVaR is unbounded.

Proof.

Consider the example of a transient MDP in Figure 3.1 with r=−1r=-1, a risk level α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), and some ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1) such that ϵ≥α\epsilon\geq\alpha. This MDP admits only a single policy because it only has one action aa, which we omit in the notation below.

Recall that the nested CVaR objective for some s≠es\neq e is

vt(s)=CVaRαs[r(s~0,a)+CVaRαs~1[r(s~1,a)+⋯CVaRαs~t−1[r(s~t−1,a)]]],v_{t}(s)\;=\;\cvaro^{s}_{\alpha}\left[r(\tilde{s}_{0},a)+\cvaro_{\alpha}^{\tilde{s}_{1}}\left[r(\tilde{s}_{1},a)+\cdots\cvaro^{\tilde{s}_{t-1}}_{\alpha}\left[r(\tilde{s}_{t-1},a)\right]\right]\right],

The value function for the non-terminal state can be computed using a dynamic program as (63, theorem 1):

vt​(s)\displaystyle v_{t}(s) =CVaRαs[r(s,a)+vt−1(s~1)]=−1+min{q1⋅vt−1(s)∣q∈Δ2,q1≤ϵα,q2≤1−ϵα}\displaystyle=\cvaro^{s}_{\alpha}[r(s,a)+v_{t-1}(\tilde{s}_{1})]=-1+\min\left\{q_{1}\cdot v_{t-1}(s)\mid q\in\Delta^{2},\,q_{1}\leq\frac{\epsilon}{\alpha},q_{2}\leq\frac{1-\epsilon}{\alpha}\right\}
≤−1−vt−1​(s).\displaystyle\leq-1-v_{t-1}(s).

Here, we used the dual representation of CVaR. Then, by induction, vt​(s)≤−tv_{t}(s)\leq-t and, therefore, limt→∞vt​(s)=−∞\lim_{t\to\infty}v_{t}(s)=-\infty. ∎

3.3  Solving ERM Total Reward Criterion

This section shows that an optimal stationary policy exists for ERM-TRC and that the value function satisfies the dynamic programming equations. We then outline algorithms for computing it.

Our objective in this section is to maximize the ERM-TRC objective for some given β>0\beta>0 defined as

supπ∈ΠHRlim inft→∞ERMβπ,𝝁⁡[∑k=0t−1r⁡(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)].\sup_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}}}\liminf_{t\to\infty}\ermo_{\beta}^{\pi,\bm{\mu}}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right]. (3.8)

The definition employs limit inferior because the limit may not exist for non-stationary policies. Return functions gt:ΠHR×ℝ+⁣+→ℝg_{t}\colon\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}}\times\mathbb{R}_{++}\to\mathbb{R} and gt⋆:ℝ+⁣+→ℝg_{t}^{\star}\colon\mathbb{R}_{++}\to\mathbb{R} for a horizon t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N} and the infinite-horizon versions gt:ΠHR×ℝ+⁣+→ℝ¯g_{t}\colon\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}}\times\mathbb{R}_{++}\to\bar{\mathbb{R}} and gt⋆:ℝ+⁣+→ℝ¯g_{t}^{\star}\colon\mathbb{R}_{++}\to\bar{\mathbb{R}} are defined

gt​(π,β)\displaystyle g_{t}(\pi,\beta) :=ERMβπ,𝝁⁡[∑k=0t−1r⁡(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)],\displaystyle:=\ermo_{\beta}^{\pi,\bm{\mu}}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right], (3.9)
gt⋆​(β)\displaystyle g_{t}^{\star}(\beta) :=supπ∈ΠHRgt​(π,β),\displaystyle:=\sup_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}}}g_{t}(\pi,\beta),
g∞​(π,β)\displaystyle g_{\infty}(\pi,\beta) :=lim inft→∞gt​(π,β),\displaystyle:=\liminf_{t\to\infty}g_{t}(\pi,\beta),
g∞⋆​(β)\displaystyle g_{\infty}^{\star}(\beta) :=lim inft→∞gt⋆​(β).\displaystyle:=\liminf_{t\to\infty}g_{t}^{\star}(\beta).

Note that the functions g∞g_{\infty} and g∞⋆g_{\infty}^{\star} can return infinite values and that (3.8) differs from g∞⋆g^{\star}_{\infty} in the order of the limit and the supremum. Finally, when β=0\beta=0, we assume that all gg functions are defined as the expectation. In the remainder of the section, we assume that the risk level β>0\beta>0 is fixed and omit it in notations when its value is unambiguous from the context.

The following lemmas show some properties of the function gg defined in  (3.9).

Lemma 3.3.1.

The functions gg defined in (3.9) satisfy for each π∈ΠSD\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}} and t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N} that

limβ→0gt​(π,β)\displaystyle\lim_{\beta\to 0}g_{t}(\pi,\beta) =gt​(π,0),\displaystyle=g_{t}(\pi,0), limβ→0gt⋆​(β)\displaystyle\lim_{\beta\to 0}g_{t}^{\star}(\beta) =gt⋆​(0),\displaystyle=g_{t}^{\star}(0),
limβ→0g∞​(π,β)\displaystyle\lim_{\beta\to 0}g_{\infty}(\pi,\beta) =g∞​(π,0),\displaystyle=g_{\infty}(\pi,0), limβ→0g∞⋆​(β)\displaystyle\lim_{\beta\to 0}g_{\infty}^{\star}(\beta) =g∞⋆​(0).\displaystyle=g_{\infty}^{\star}(0).
Proof.

The result for gtg_{t} holds from the continuity of ERM as β→0+\beta\to 0^{+}; e.g.  (49, remark 2.8). The result for gt⋆g_{t}^{\star} then follows from the fact that ΠSD\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}} is finite. Then, (113, lemma 1) shows that there exists β0>0\beta_{0}>0 such that gt→g∞g_{t}\to g_{\infty} uniformly on (0,β0)(0,\beta_{0}) and the limits can be exchanged. Therefore, the result also holds for g∞g_{\infty} and g∞⋆g_{\infty}^{\star}. ∎

Lemma 3.3.2.

The functions gg defined in (3.9) are monotonically non-increasing in the parameter β≥0\beta\geq 0.

Proof.

This well-known result follows, for example, from the dual representation of ERM [39]. ∎

3.3.1  Finite Horizon

We commence the analysis with definitions and basic properties for the finite horizon criterion. To the best of our knowledge, this analysis is original in the context of the ERM but builds on similar approaches employed in the study of exponential utility functions.

Finite-horizon functions 𝒗t​(π)∈ℝS\bm{v}^{t}(\pi)\in\mathbb{R}^{S} and 𝒗t,⋆∈ℝS\bm{v}^{t,\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{S} are defined for each horizon t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N} and policy π∈ΠMD\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{MD}}, s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} as

vst​(π)\displaystyle v^{t}_{s}(\pi) :=ERMβπ,s⁡[∑k=0t−1r⁡(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)],\displaystyle:=\;\ermo_{\beta}^{\pi,s}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right], (3.10)
vst,⋆\displaystyle v^{t,\star}_{s} :=maxπ∈ΠMD⁡vst​(π),\displaystyle:=\;\max_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{MD}}}v^{t}_{s}(\pi),

and vet​(π):=0v_{e}^{t}(\pi):=0.

Because the nonlinearity of ERM complicates the analysis, it will be convenient to instead rely on exponential value function 𝒘t​(π)∈ℝS\bm{w}^{t}(\pi)\in\mathbb{R}^{S} for π∈ΠMD\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{MD}}, t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}, and s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} that satisfy

wst​(π)\displaystyle w_{s}^{t}(\pi) :=−exp(−β⋅vst(π)),\displaystyle:=-\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot v_{s}^{t}(\pi)\right), (3.11)
vst​(π)\displaystyle v^{t}_{s}(\pi) =−β−1​log⁡(−wst​(π)).\displaystyle=-\beta^{-1}\log(-w^{t}_{s}(\pi)). (3.12)

The optimal 𝒘t,⋆∈ℝS\bm{w}^{t,\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{S} is defined analogously from 𝒗t,⋆\bm{v}^{t,\star}. Note that 𝒘t<𝟎\bm{w}^{t}<\bm{0} (componentwise) and 𝒘0​(π)=𝒘0,⋆=−𝟏\bm{w}^{0}(\pi)=\bm{w}^{0,\star}=-\bm{1} for any π∈ΠMD\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{MD}}. Similar exponential value functions have been used previously in exponential utility function objectives [53, 113], in the analysis of robust MDPs, and even in regularized MDPs (see [114] and references therein).

One can define a corresponding exponential Bellman operator for any 𝒘∈ℝS\bm{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{S} as

L𝒅​𝒘\displaystyle L^{\bm{d}}\bm{w} :=𝑩𝒅​𝒘−𝒃𝒅,\displaystyle:=\;\bm{B}^{\bm{d}}\bm{w}-\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}, (3.13)
L⋆​𝒘\displaystyle L^{\star}\bm{w} :=max𝒅∈𝒟⁡L𝒅​𝒘=max𝒅∈ext⁡𝒟⁡L𝒅​𝒘,\displaystyle:=\;\max_{\bm{d}\in\mathcal{D}}L^{\bm{d}}\bm{w}=\max_{\bm{d}\in\ext\mathcal{D}}L^{\bm{d}}\bm{w},

where ext⁡𝒟\ext\mathcal{D} is the set of extreme points of 𝒟\mathcal{D} corresponding to deterministic decision rules and 𝑩𝒅∈ℝ+S×S\bm{B}^{\bm{d}}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{S\times S} and 𝒃𝒅∈ℝ+S\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{S} are defined for s,s′∈𝒮s,s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S} and 𝒅∈𝒟\bm{d}\in\mathcal{D} as

Bs,s′𝒅\displaystyle B_{s,s^{\prime}}^{\bm{d}} :=∑a∈𝒜p(s,a,s′)⋅da(s)⋅e−β⋅r(s,a,s′),\displaystyle:=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}p(s,a,s^{\prime})\cdot d_{a}(s)\cdot e^{-\beta\cdot r(s,a,s^{\prime})}, (3.14a)
bs𝒅\displaystyle b_{s}^{\bm{d}} :=∑a∈𝒜p(s,a,e)⋅da(s)⋅e−β⋅r(s,a,e).\displaystyle:=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}p(s,a,e)\cdot d_{a}(s)\cdot e^{-\beta\cdot r(s,a,e)}. (3.14b)

We state some properties of the exponential Bellman operator in Lemma 3.3.3 and Lemma 3.3.4.

Lemma 3.3.3.

The exponential Bellman operator is monotone. That is, for 𝐱,𝐲∈ℝS\bm{x},\bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{S}

𝒙≥𝒚\displaystyle\bm{x}\geq\bm{y} ⇒L𝒅​𝒙≥L𝒅​𝒚,∀𝒅∈𝒟\displaystyle\quad\Rightarrow\quad L^{\bm{d}}\bm{x}\geq L^{\bm{d}}\bm{y},\qquad\forall\bm{d}\in\mathcal{D} (3.15)
𝒙≥𝒚\displaystyle\bm{x}\geq\bm{y} ⇒L⋆​𝒙≥L⋆​𝒚.\displaystyle\quad\Rightarrow\quad L^{\star}\bm{x}\geq L^{\star}\bm{y}. (3.16)
Proof.

The property in (3.15) follows immediately from non-negativity of 𝑩𝒅\bm{B}^{\bm{d}}. The property in (3.16) then follows from the monotonicity of the max\max operator. ∎

Lemma 3.3.4.

The exponential Bellman operators L𝐝,∀𝐝∈𝒟L^{\bm{d}},\,\forall\bm{d}\in\mathcal{D} and L⋆L^{\star} are continuous.

Proof.

The lemma follows directly from the continuity of linear operators and from the fact that the pointwise maximum of a finite number of continuous functions is continuous. See also (113, lemma 5) ∎

The following theorem shows that LL can be used to compute 𝒘\bm{w}. We use the shorthand notation π1:t−1=(𝒅1,…,𝒅t−1)∈ΠMRt−1\pi_{1{:}t{-}1}=(\bm{d}_{1},\dots,\bm{d}_{t-1})\in\Pi_{\mathrm{MR}}^{t-1} to denote the tail of π\pi that starts with 𝒅1\bm{d}_{1} instead of 𝒅0\bm{d}_{0}.

Theorem 3.3.5.

For each t=1,…t=1,\dots, and π=(𝐝0,…,𝐝t−1)∈ΠMRt\pi=(\bm{d}_{0},\dots,\bm{d}_{t-1})\in\Pi_{\mathrm{MR}}^{t}, the exponential values satisfy that

𝒘t​(π)\displaystyle\bm{w}^{t}(\pi) =L𝒅t𝒘t−1(π1:t−1),\displaystyle=L^{\bm{d}_{t}}\bm{w}^{t-1}(\pi_{1{:}t{-}1}), 𝒘0​(π)\displaystyle\bm{w}^{0}(\pi) =−𝟏,\displaystyle=-\bm{1},
𝒘t,⋆\displaystyle\bm{w}^{t,\star} =L⋆​𝒘t−1,⋆=𝒘t​(π⋆)≥𝒘t​(π),\displaystyle=L^{\star}\bm{w}^{t-1,\star}=\bm{w}^{t}(\pi^{\star})\geq\bm{w}^{t}(\pi), 𝒘0,⋆\displaystyle\bm{w}^{0,\star} =−𝟏,\displaystyle=-\bm{1},

for some π⋆∈ΠMDt\pi^{\star}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{MD}}^{t}.

The proof of Theorem 3.3.5 is standard and has been established both in the context of ERMs [39] and exponential utility functions [115].

Proof of Theorem 3.3.5.

To construct the value function, we can define a Bellman operator T𝒅:ℝS→ℝST^{\bm{d}}\colon\mathbb{R}^{S}\to\mathbb{R}^{S} for any decision rule 𝒅:𝒮→ΔA\bm{d}\colon\mathcal{S}\to\Delta_{A} and the optimal Bellman operator T⋆:ℝS→ℝST^{\star}\colon\mathbb{R}^{S}\to\mathbb{R}^{S} for a value vector 𝒗∈ℝS\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{S} as

(T𝒅​𝒗)s\displaystyle(T^{\bm{d}}\bm{v})_{s} :=ERMβ𝒅,s⁡[r⁡(s,a~0,s~1)+vs~1],\displaystyle:=\;\ermo_{\beta}^{\bm{d},s}\left[r(s,\tilde{a}_{0},\tilde{s}_{1})+v_{\tilde{s}_{1}}\right], (3.17)
T⋆​𝒗\displaystyle T^{\star}\bm{v} :=max𝒅∈𝒟⁡T𝒅​𝒗=max𝒅∈ext⁡𝒟⁡T𝒅​𝒗.\displaystyle:=\;\max_{\bm{d}\in\mathcal{D}}T^{\bm{d}}\bm{v}=\max_{\bm{d}\in\ext\mathcal{D}}T^{\bm{d}}\bm{v}.

It is easy to see that 𝒅\bm{d} in (3.17) can be chosen independently for each state to maximize 𝒗\bm{v} uniformly across states. The optimality of deterministic decision rules, 𝒅∈ext⁡𝒟\bm{d}\in\ext\mathcal{D}, follows because ERM is a mixture quasi-convex function [116].

The existence of a value function for a finite-horizon problem under the ERM objective has been analyzed previously [39], including in the context of exponential utility functions [112].

To derive the exponential Bellman operator for the exponential value function for 𝒅:𝒮→ΔA\bm{d}\colon\mathcal{S}\to\Delta_{A}, we concatenate the Bellman operator with the transformations to and from the exponential value function:

(L𝒅​𝒘)s\displaystyle(L^{\bm{d}}\bm{w})_{s} =−exp(−β⋅T𝒅(−β−1log(−𝒘)))\displaystyle=\;-\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot T^{\bm{d}}(-\beta^{-1}\log(-\bm{w}))\right) (3.18)
=−𝔼𝒅,s[exp(−β⋅r(s,a~0,s~1)+log(−ws~1))]\displaystyle=\;-\mathbb{E}^{\bm{d},s}\left[\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot r(s,\tilde{a}_{0},\tilde{s}_{1})+\log(-w_{\tilde{s}_{1}})\right)\right]
=−𝔼𝒅,s[exp(−β⋅r(s,a~0,s~1))⋅(−ws~1)]\displaystyle=\;-\mathbb{E}^{\bm{d},s}\left[\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot r(s,\tilde{a}_{0},\tilde{s}_{1})\right)\cdot(-w_{\tilde{s}_{1}})\right]
=∑s′∈𝒮¯∑a∈𝒜p(s,a,s′)⋅da(s)⋅exp(−β⋅r(s,a,s′))⋅ws′\displaystyle=\;\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\bar{\mathcal{S}}}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}p(s,a,s^{\prime})\cdot d_{a}(s)\cdot\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot r(s,a,s^{\prime})\right)\cdot w_{s^{\prime}}
=∑s′∈𝒮∑a∈𝒜p(s,a,s′)⋅da(s)⋅exp(−β⋅r(s,a,s′))⋅ws′\displaystyle=\;\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}p(s,a,s^{\prime})\cdot d_{a}(s)\cdot\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot r(s,a,s^{\prime})\right)\cdot w_{s^{\prime}}
−∑a∈𝒜p(s,a,e)⋅da(s)⋅exp(−β⋅r(s,a,e)).\displaystyle-\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}p(s,a,e)\cdot d_{a}(s)\cdot\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot r(s,a,e)\right).

The derivation above uses the fact that we=−1w_{e}=-1 since ve=0v_{e}=0 by definition. The statement of the theorem then follows by algebraic manipulation of 𝑩𝒅,𝒃𝒅\bm{B}^{\bm{d}},\bm{b}^{\bm{d}} and by induction on tt. The base case hold by the definition of 𝒘0​(π)=𝒘0,⋆=−𝟏\bm{w}^{0}(\pi)=\bm{w}^{0,\star}=-\bm{1}.

The existence of an optimal π⋆\pi^{\star} follows by choosing the maximum in the definition of L⋆L^{\star}, which is attained by compactness and continuity of the objective. ∎

The following corollary follows directly from Theorem 3.3.5 by algebraic manipulation and by the monotonicity of exponential value function transformation and the ERM.

Corollary 3.3.6.

We have that

gt​(π,β)\displaystyle g_{t}(\pi,\beta) =ERMβ𝝁​[vs~0t​(π)],\displaystyle=\ermo^{\bm{\mu}}_{\beta}\left[v^{t}_{\tilde{s}_{0}}(\pi)\right],
gt⋆​(β)\displaystyle g_{t}^{\star}(\beta) =ERMβ𝝁​[vs~0t,⋆]=maxπ∈ΠMD⁡ERMβ𝝁​[vs~0t​(π)].\displaystyle=\ermo^{\bm{\mu}}_{\beta}\left[v^{t,\star}_{\tilde{s}_{0}}\right]=\max_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{MD}}}\ermo^{\bm{\mu}}_{\beta}\left[v^{t}_{\tilde{s}_{0}}(\pi)\right].

In a discounted MDP, the discount factor ensures that the ERM value function is always bounded. However, for the total-reward criterion, the ERM value function can be unbounded, as shown in Proposition 3.3.7.

Proposition 3.3.7.

There exists a transient MDP and a risk level β>0\beta>0 such that g∞⋆​(β)=−∞g_{\infty}^{\star}(\beta)=-\infty.

Proof.

We use the transient MDP described in Figure 3.1 to show this result. Because the returns of this MDP follow a truncated geometric distribution, its risk-averse return for each β>0\beta>0 and ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1) can be expressed analytically for t≥1t\geq 1 as

ERMβπ⁡[∑k=0t−1r⁡(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)]\displaystyle\ermo_{\beta}^{\pi}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right] =−1βlog(∑k=0t−1(1−ϵ)ϵk⋅exp(−β⋅k⋅r)+ϵt⋅0)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\beta}\log\left(\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}(1-\epsilon)\epsilon^{k}\cdot\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot k\cdot r\right)+\epsilon^{t}\cdot 0\right) (3.19)
=−1βlog(∑k=0t−1(1−ϵ)ϵk⋅exp(−β⋅r)k).\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\beta}\log\left(\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}(1-\epsilon)\epsilon^{k}\cdot\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot r\right)^{k}\right).

Here, (1−ϵ)​ϵk(1-\epsilon)\epsilon^{k} is the probability that the process terminates after exactly kk steps, and ϵt\epsilon^{t} is the probability that the process does not terminate before reaching the horizon. Then, using the fact that a geometric series ∑i=0∞a⋅qi\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}a\cdot q^{i} for a≠0a\neq 0 is bounded if and only if |q|<1|q|<1 we get that

limt→∞ERMβπ[∑k=0t−1r(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)]>−∞⇔ϵ⋅exp(−β⋅r)<1.\lim_{t\to\infty}\ermo_{\beta}^{\pi}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right]>-\infty\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad\epsilon\cdot\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot r\right)<1.

Note that ϵ⋅exp(−β⋅r)≥0\epsilon\cdot\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot r\right)\geq 0 from its definition. Then, setting r=−1r=-1 and β>−log⁡ϵ\beta>-\log\epsilon proves the result. ∎

Unlike the risk-neutral setting, for risk-averse objectives, such as ERM, the value functions of a discounted MDP can differ from those in a transient MDP, as the following proposition shows.

Proposition 3.3.8.

There exists an MDP ℳ\mathcal{M}, γ>0\gamma>0, β>0\beta>0, ℳ¯γ\bar{\mathcal{M}}_{\gamma} constructed in Section 3.2, and π∈ΠSD\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}} such that

ργ​(π,β)≠g∞​(π,β),\rho_{\gamma}(\pi,\beta)\;\neq\;g_{\infty}(\pi,\beta),

where ργ​(π,0)\rho_{\gamma}(\pi,0) is defined in (3.3) and g∞​(π,0)g_{\infty}(\pi,0) is defined in (3.9).

Proof.

See the one-state example described in Section 3.5. ∎

3.3.2  Infinite Horizon

We now turn to constructing infinite-horizon optimal policies as a limiting case of the finite-horizon case. An important quantity is the infinite-horizon exponential value function defined for each π∈ΠHR\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}} as

𝒘∞​(π):=lim inft→∞𝒘t​(π),𝒘∞,⋆:=lim inft→∞𝒘t,⋆.\bm{w}^{\infty}(\pi)\;:=\;\liminf_{t\to\infty}\bm{w}^{t}(\pi),\quad\bm{w}^{\infty,\star}\;:=\;\liminf_{t\to\infty}\bm{w}^{t,\star}.

Note again that we use the inferior limit because the limit may not be defined for non-stationary policies. The limiting infinite-horizon value functions 𝒘∞​(π)\bm{w}^{\infty}(\pi) and 𝒘∞,⋆\bm{w}^{\infty,\star} are defined analogously from 𝒗t​(π)\bm{v}^{t}(\pi) and 𝒗t,⋆\bm{v}^{t,\star} using the inferior limit. The following theorem is the main result of this section. It shows that for an infinite horizon, the optimal exponential value function is attained by a stationary deterministic policy and is a fixed point of the exponential Bellman operator.

Theorem 3.3.9.

Whenever 𝐰∞,⋆>−∞\bm{w}^{\infty,\star}>-\bm{\infty} there exists π⋆=(𝐝⋆)∞∈ΠSD\pi^{\star}=(\bm{d}^{\star})_{\infty}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}} such that

𝒘∞,⋆=𝒘∞​(π⋆)=L𝒅⋆​𝒘∞,⋆,\bm{w}^{\infty,\star}\;=\;\bm{w}^{\infty}(\pi^{\star})\;=\;L^{\bm{d}^{\star}}\bm{w}^{\infty,\star},

and 𝐰∞,⋆\bm{w}^{\infty,\star} is the unique value that satisfies this equation.

The main idea of the proof of Theorem 3.3.9 is to show that whenever the exponential value functions are bounded, the exponential Bellman operator must be weighted-norm contraction with a unique fixed point. To facilitate the analysis, we define 𝒘t:ΠSRt×ℝS→ℝS,t∈ℕ\bm{w}^{t}\colon\Pi_{\mathrm{SR}}^{t}\times\mathbb{R}^{S}\to\mathbb{R}^{S},t\in\mathbb{N} for 𝒛∈ℝS,π∈ΠSRt\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{S},\,\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SR}}^{t}, as

𝒘t​(π,𝒛)=\displaystyle\bm{w}^{t}(\pi,\bm{z})\;= L𝒅𝒘(π1:t−1)=L𝒅L𝒅…L𝒅(−𝒛)\displaystyle L^{\bm{d}}\bm{w}(\pi_{1{:}t{-}1})\;=\;L^{\bm{d}}L^{\bm{d}}\dots L^{\bm{d}}(-\bm{z}) (3.20)
=\displaystyle\;= −(𝑩𝒅)t​𝒛−∑k=0t−1(𝑩𝒅)k​𝒃𝒅.\displaystyle-(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})^{t}\bm{\bm{z}}-\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})^{k}\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}.

The value 𝒛\bm{z} can be interpreted as the exponential value function at the termination of the process following π\pi for tt periods. Note that 𝒘t​(π)=𝒘t​(π,𝟏),∀π∈ΠMR,t∈ℕ.\bm{w}^{t}(\pi)=\bm{w}^{t}(\pi,\bm{1}),\,\forall\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{MR}},t\in\mathbb{N}.

We now outline the proof of Theorem 3.3.9; see (67, appendix D.4) for details. To establish Theorem 3.3.9, we show that 𝒘t,⋆\bm{w}^{t,\star} converges to a fixed point as t→∞t\to\infty. Standard arguments do not apply to our setting [106, 4, 113] because the ERM-TRC Bellman operator is not an L∞L_{\infty}-contraction, it is not linear, and the values in value iteration do not increase or decrease monotonically. Although the exponential Bellman operator L𝒅L^{\bm{d}} is linear, it may not be a contraction.

Now we state Lemma 3.3.10 and Theorem 3.3.11 that are useful for the formal proof of Theorem 3.3.9.

Lemma 3.3.10.

Assume some π=(𝐝)∞∈ΠSR\pi=(\bm{d})_{\infty}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SR}} such that ρ⁡(𝐁𝐝)<1\rho(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})<1. Then for all 𝐳∈ℝS\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{S}

𝒘∞​(π)=𝒘∞​(π,𝒛)=L𝒅​𝒘∞​(π)>−∞.\bm{w}^{\infty}(\pi)=\bm{w}^{\infty}(\pi,\bm{z})=L^{\bm{d}}\bm{w}^{\infty}(\pi)>-\bm{\infty}.
Proof.

The result follows by algebraic manipulation from (3.20) and basic matrix analysis. When ρ⁡(𝑩𝒅)<1\rho(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})<1, we get from Neumann series (110, problem 5.6.P26)

limt→∞∑k=0t−1(𝑩𝒅)k​𝒃𝒅=(𝑰−𝑩𝒅)−1​𝒃𝒅,\lim_{t\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})^{k}\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}=(\bm{I}-\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})^{-1}\bm{b}^{\bm{d}},

and a consequence of Gelfand’s formula (4, theorem 4.5)

limk→∞(𝑩𝒅)k​𝒛=𝟎.\lim_{k\to\infty}(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})^{k}\bm{z}=\bm{0}.

∎

Theorem 3.3.11 can be derived from the optimality of Markov deterministic policies in MDPs with exponential utility functions [112, 113].

Theorem 3.3.11.

For each β>0\beta>0, there exists an optimal deterministic Markov policy πt,⋆∈ΠMD\pi^{t,\star}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{MD}} for each horizon t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}:

maxπ∈ΠMD⁡ERMβπ,s​[∑k=0t−1r⁡(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)]=maxπ∈ΠHR⁡ERMβπ,s​[∑k=0t−1r⁡(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)].\begin{split}\max_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{MD}}}\ermo_{\beta}^{\pi,s}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right]\;=\;\max_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}}}\ermo_{\beta}^{\pi,s}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right].\end{split}

See (39, Corollary 4.2) for a proof.

We are ready to prove Theorem 3.3.9.

Proof of Theorem 3.3.9.

Let πM⋆∈arg⁡maxπ∈ΠMR​𝝁⊤​𝒗∞​(π)\pi_{\mathrm{M}}^{\star}\in\arg\max_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{MR}}}\bm{\mu}^{\top}\bm{v}^{\infty}(\pi) and suppose that 𝝁⊤​𝒗∞​(πM⋆)>−∞\bm{\mu}^{\top}\bm{v}^{\infty}(\pi^{\star}_{\mathrm{M}})>-\infty. Then, the exponential value function 𝒘t,⋆=𝒘t​(πM⋆)∈ℝS\bm{w}^{t,\star}=\bm{w}^{t}(\pi_{\mathrm{M}}^{\star})\in\mathbb{R}^{S} of πM⋆\pi_{\mathrm{M}}^{\star} satisfies by Theorem 3.3.5 that

𝒘0,⋆=−𝟏,𝒘t(πM⋆)=L⋆𝒘t−1(πM⋆),t=1,….\bm{w}^{0,\star}=-\bm{1},\qquad\bm{w}^{t}(\pi^{\star}_{\mathrm{M}})=L^{\star}\bm{w}^{t-1}(\pi^{\star}_{\mathrm{M}}),\quad t=1,\dots.

We show that limt→∞𝒘t,⋆\lim_{t\to\infty}\bm{w}^{t,\star} exists and that a stationary policy attains it. We construct a sequence 𝒘ut∈ℝS,t∈ℕ\bm{w}_{\mathrm{u}}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{S},t\in\mathbb{N} as

𝒘u0=𝟎,𝒘ut=L⋆𝒘ut−1,t=1,….\bm{w}_{\mathrm{u}}^{0}=\bm{0},\qquad\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t}=L^{\star}\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t-1},\quad t=1,\dots.

First, we show by induction that

𝒘ut≥𝒘t,⋆,t∈ℕ.\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t}\quad\geq\quad\bm{w}^{t,\star},\qquad t\in\mathbb{N}. (3.21)

The base case t=0t=0 follows immediately from the definitions of 𝒘u0\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{0} and 𝒘0,⋆\bm{w}^{0,\star}. Next, suppose that (3.21) holds for some t>0t>0, then it also holds for t+1t+1:

𝒘ut+1=L⋆​𝒘ut≥L⋆​𝒘t,⋆=𝒘t+1,⋆,\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t+1}\;=\;L^{\star}\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t}\;\geq\;L^{\star}\bm{w}^{t,\star}\;=\;\bm{w}^{t+1,\star},

where the inequality follows from the inductive assumption and from Lemma 3.3.3. Second, we show by induction that

𝒘ut+1≤𝒘ut,t∈ℕ.\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t+1}\quad\leq\quad\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t},\qquad t\in\mathbb{N}. (3.22)

The base case for t=0t=0 holds as

𝒘u1=L⋆​𝒘u0=L⋆​𝟎=max𝒅∈𝒟−𝒃𝒅≤ 0=𝒘u0,\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{1}\;=\;L^{\star}\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{0}\;=\;L^{\star}\bm{0}\;=\;\max_{\bm{d}\in\mathcal{D}}-\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}\;\leq\;\bm{0}\;=\;\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{0},

where the inequality holds because 𝒃𝒅≥0\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}\geq 0 from its construction. To prove the inductive step, assume that (3.22) holds for t>0t>0 and prove it for t+1t+1:

𝒘ut+1=L⋆​𝒘ut≤L⋆​𝒘ut−1=𝒘ut,\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t+1}\;=\;L^{\star}\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t}\;\leq\;L^{\star}\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t-1}\;=\;\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t},

where the inequality follows from the inductive assumption and from Lemma 3.3.3.

Then, using the Monotone Convergence Theorem (117, theorem 16.2), finite 𝒮\mathcal{S}, and inft∈ℕ𝒘ut≥inft∈ℕ𝒘t,⋆>−∞\inf_{t\in\mathbb{N}}\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t}\geq\inf_{t\in\mathbb{N}}\bm{w}^{t,\star}>-\infty, we get that there exists 𝒘u⋆∈ℝS\bm{w}_{\mathrm{u}}^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{S} such that

𝒘u⋆=limt→∞𝒘ut,\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{\star}=\lim_{t\to\infty}\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t},

and the limit exists. Then, taking the limit of both sides of 𝒘ut=L⋆​𝒘ut−1\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t}=L^{\star}\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t-1}, we have that

limt→∞𝒘ut\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t} =limt→∞L⋆​𝒘ut−1\displaystyle=\lim_{t\to\infty}L^{\star}\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t-1}
𝒘u⋆\displaystyle\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{\star} =limt→∞L⋆​𝒘ut−1\displaystyle=\lim_{t\to\infty}L^{\star}\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t-1}
𝒘u⋆\displaystyle\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{\star} =L⋆​limt→∞𝒘ut−1\displaystyle=L^{\star}\lim_{t\to\infty}\bm{w}_{\textrm{u}}^{t-1}
𝒘u⋆\displaystyle\bm{w}_{\mathrm{u}}^{\star} =L𝒅⋆​𝒘u⋆,\displaystyle=L^{\bm{d}^{\star}}\bm{w}_{\mathrm{u}}^{\star},

where 𝒅⋆=argmax𝒅∈𝒟L𝒅​𝒘u\bm{d}^{\star}=\argmax_{\bm{d}\in\mathcal{D}}L^{\bm{d}}\bm{w}_{\mathrm{u}}. Above, we can exchange the operators L⋆L^{\star} and lim\lim by the continuity of L⋆L^{\star} (Lemma 3.3.4).

Now, define 𝒘lt∈ℝS,t∈ℕ\bm{w}_{\mathrm{l}}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{S},t\in\mathbb{N} as

𝒘l0=−𝟏,𝒘lt=L𝒅⋆𝒘lt−1,t=1,….\bm{w}_{\mathrm{l}}^{0}=-\bm{1},\qquad\bm{w}_{\textrm{l}}^{t}=L^{\bm{d}^{\star}}\bm{w}_{\textrm{l}}^{t-1},\quad t=1,\dots.

From the definition of L⋆L^{\star} and by induction on tt we have that.

𝒘lt≤𝒘t,⋆.\bm{w}_{\mathrm{l}}^{t}\leq\bm{w}^{t,\star}.

By Lemma 3.3.13 for 𝒛=𝟎\bm{z}=\bm{0}, we have that ρ⁡(𝑩𝒅⋆)<1\rho(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}^{\star}})<1 and therefore from Lemma 3.3.10

limt→∞𝒘lt=limt→∞𝒘ut=𝒘u⋆.\lim_{t\to\infty}\bm{w}_{\mathrm{l}}^{t}=\lim_{t\to\infty}\bm{w}_{\mathrm{u}}^{t}=\bm{w}_{\mathrm{u}}^{\star}.

In addition, because

𝒘ut≥𝒘t,⋆≥𝒘lt,t∈ℕ,\bm{w}_{\mathrm{u}}^{t}\;\geq\;\bm{w}^{t,\star}\;\geq\;\bm{w}_{\mathrm{l}}^{t},\qquad t\in\mathbb{N},

the Squeeze Theorem (117, theorem 14.3) shows that

limt→∞𝒘t,⋆=𝒘u⋆,\lim_{t\to\infty}\bm{w}^{t,\star}=\bm{w}_{\mathrm{u}}^{\star},

and 𝒅⋆\bm{d}^{\star} is a stationary policy that attains the return of πM⋆\pi^{\star}_{\mathrm{M}}. ∎

Corollary 3.3.12.

Assuming the hypothesis of Theorem 3.3.9, we have that 𝒗∞,⋆=𝒗∞​(π⋆)\bm{v}^{\infty,\star}=\bm{v}^{\infty}(\pi^{\star}) and

g∞⋆​(β)=ERMβ𝝁​[vs~0∞,⋆]=maxπ∈ΠSD⁡ERMβ𝝁​[vs~0∞​(π)].g_{\infty}^{\star}(\beta)=\ermo^{\bm{\mu}}_{\beta}\left[v^{\infty,\star}_{\tilde{s}_{0}}\right]=\max_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}}}\ermo^{\bm{\mu}}_{\beta}\left[v^{\infty}_{\tilde{s}_{0}}(\pi)\right].
Proof of Corollary 3.3.12.

From the existence of an optimal stationary policy π⋆∈ΠSD\pi^{\star}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}} from for a sufficiently large horizon tt from Theorem 3.3.9 and , we get that

𝝁⊤​𝒗∞​(π⋆)≤supπ∈ΠHRlim inft→∞𝝁⊤​𝒗t​(π)≤lim inft→∞supπ∈ΠHRt𝝁⊤​𝒗t​(π)≤𝝁⊤​𝒗∞​(π⋆),\displaystyle\bm{\mu}^{\top}\bm{v}^{\infty}(\pi^{\star})\leq\sup_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}}}\liminf_{t\to\infty}\bm{\mu}^{\top}\bm{v}^{t}(\pi)\leq\liminf_{t\to\infty}\sup_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}}^{t}}\bm{\mu}^{\top}\bm{v}^{t}(\pi)\leq\bm{\mu}^{\top}\bm{v}^{\infty}(\pi^{\star}),

which implies that all inequalities above hold with equality. ∎

An important technical result we show is that the only way a stationary policy’s return can be bounded is if the policy’s matrix has a spectral radius strictly less than 11.

Lemma 3.3.13.

For each π=(𝐝)∞∈ΠSR\pi=(\bm{d})_{\infty}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SR}} and 𝐳≥𝟎\bm{z}\geq\bm{0}:

𝒘∞(π,𝒛)>−∞⇔ρ(𝑩𝒅)<1.\bm{w}^{\infty}(\pi,\bm{z})>-\bm{\infty}\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\rho(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})<1.

Lemma 3.3.13 uses the transience property to show that the Perron vector (with the maximum absolute eigenvalue) 𝒇\bm{f} of 𝑩𝒅\bm{B}^{\bm{d}} satisfies that 𝒇⊤​𝒃𝒅>0\bm{f}^{\top}\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}>0. Therefore, ρ⁡(𝑩𝒅)<1\rho(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})<1 is necessary for the series in (3.20) to be bounded.

We state Lemma 3.3.14, Lemma 3.3.15, Lemma 3.3.16, and Lemma 3.3.17 that are useful in the proof of Lemma 3.3.13. We use 𝒑𝒅∈ℝ+S\bm{p}^{\bm{d}}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{S} to represent the probability of terminating from any state for each 𝒅∈𝒟\bm{d}\in\mathcal{D}:

ps𝒅=∑a∈𝒜da​(s)⋅p¯​(s,a,e),∀s∈𝒮.p^{\bm{d}}_{s}=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}d_{a}(s)\cdot\bar{p}(s,a,e),\quad\forall s\in\mathcal{S}.

The following lemma establishes a convenient representation of the termination probabilities.

Lemma 3.3.14.

Assume a policy π=(𝐝)∞∈ΠSR\pi=(\bm{d})_{\infty}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SR}}. Then, the probability of terminating in t∈ℕ,t>0t\in\mathbb{N},t>0 or fewer steps is

∑k=0t−1𝝁⊤​(𝑷𝒅)k​𝒑𝒅=𝝁⊤​(𝑰−(𝑷𝒅)t)​𝟏,\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\bm{\mu}^{\top}(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{k}\bm{p}^{\bm{d}}\;=\;\bm{\mu}^{\top}(\bm{I}-(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{t})\bm{1},

where 𝐏𝐝\bm{P}^{\bm{d}} is a |𝒮|×|𝒮||\mathcal{S}|\times|\mathcal{S}| matrix, and each element Ps,s′𝐝=∑a∈𝒜da​(s)⋅p⁡(s,a,s′),∀s,s′∈𝒮P^{\bm{d}}_{s,s^{\prime}}=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}d_{a}(s)\cdot p(s,a,s^{\prime}),\forall s,s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}.

Proof.

We have by algebraic manipulation that

𝒑𝒅=(𝑰−𝑷𝒅)​𝟏.\bm{p}^{\bm{d}}=(\bm{I}-\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})\bm{1}.

The probability of terminating in step t>0t>0 exactly is

𝝁⊤​(𝑷𝒅)t−1​𝒑𝒅.\bm{\mu}^{\top}(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{t-1}\bm{p}^{\bm{d}}.

Using algebraic manipulation and recognizing a telescopic sum, we have that the probability of terminating in k≤tk\leq t steps is

∑k=0t−1𝝁⊤​(𝑷𝒅)k​𝒑𝒅=∑k=0t−1𝝁⊤​(𝑷𝒅)k​(𝑰−𝑷𝒅)​𝟏=𝝁⊤​(𝑰−(𝑷𝒅)t)​𝟏.\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\bm{\mu}^{\top}(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{k}\bm{p}^{\bm{d}}=\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\bm{\mu}^{\top}(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{k}(\bm{I}-\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})\bm{1}=\bm{\mu}^{\top}(\bm{I}-(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{t})\bm{1}.

∎

Lemma 3.3.15.

For any 𝐝∈𝒟\bm{d}\in\mathcal{D}, the exponential transition matrix is monotone:

𝒙≥𝒚⇒𝑩𝒅​𝒙≥𝑩𝒅​𝒚,∀𝒙,𝒚∈ℝS.\bm{x}\geq\bm{y}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\bm{B}^{\bm{d}}\bm{x}\geq\bm{B}^{\bm{d}}\bm{y},\qquad\forall\bm{x},\bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{S}.
Proof.

The result follows immediately from the fact that 𝑩𝒅\bm{B}^{\bm{d}} is a non-nonnegative matrix. ∎

Lemma 3.3.16.

For each t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N} and each policy π=(𝐝)∞∈ΠSR\pi=(\bm{d})_{\infty}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SR}} and each 𝛈∈ΔS\bm{\eta}\in\Delta_{S}:

𝜼⊤(𝑩𝒅)t𝒃𝒅=0⇔𝜼⊤(𝑷𝒅)t𝒑𝒅=0.\bm{\eta}^{\top}(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})^{t}\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}=0\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad\bm{\eta}^{\top}(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{t}\bm{p}^{\bm{d}}=0. (3.23)
Proof.

Algebraic manipulation from the definition in (3.14) shows that

cl⋅𝒑𝒅≤𝒃𝒅≤cu⋅𝒑𝒅,cl⋅𝑷𝒅​𝒙≤𝑩𝒅​𝒙≤cu⋅𝑷𝒅𝒙,∀𝒙∈ℝS,\begin{array}[]{rcl}c_{\mathrm{l}}\cdot\bm{p}^{\bm{d}}\;\leq&\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}&\;\leq\;c_{\mathrm{u}}\cdot\bm{p}^{\bm{d}},\\ c_{\mathrm{l}}\cdot\bm{P}^{\bm{d}}\bm{x}\;\leq&\bm{B}^{\bm{d}}\bm{x}&\;\leq\;c_{\mathrm{u}}\cdot\bm{P}^{\bm{d}}\bm{x},\qquad\forall\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{S},\end{array} (3.24)

where

cl:=mins,s′∈𝒮¯,a∈𝒜exp(−β⋅r(s,a,s′)),\displaystyle c_{\mathrm{l}}:=\min_{s,s^{\prime}\in\bar{\mathcal{S}},a\in\mathcal{A}}\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot r(s,a,s^{\prime})\right),
cu:=maxs,s′∈𝒮¯,a∈𝒜exp(−β⋅r(s,a,s′)).\displaystyle c_{\mathrm{u}}:=\max_{s,s^{\prime}\in\bar{\mathcal{S}},a\in\mathcal{A}}\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot r(s,a,s^{\prime})\right).

Note that ∞>cu>cl>0\infty>c_{\mathrm{u}}>c_{\mathrm{l}}>0.

We now extend the inequalities in (3.24) to multiple time steps. Suppose that 𝒚l≤𝒚≤𝒚u\bm{y}_{\mathrm{l}}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{y}_{\mathrm{u}}, then, for t=ℕt=\mathbb{N}:

clt⋅(𝑷𝒅)t​𝒚l≤(𝑩𝒅)t​𝒚≤cut⋅(𝑷𝒅)t​𝒚u.c_{\mathrm{l}}^{t}\cdot(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{t}\bm{y}_{\mathrm{l}}\;\leq\;(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})^{t}\bm{y}\;\leq\;c_{\mathrm{u}}^{t}\cdot(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{t}\bm{y}_{\mathrm{u}}. (3.25)

For the left inequality in (3.25), the induction proceeds as follows. The base case t=0t=0 holds immediately. For the inductive step, suppose that the left inequality in (3.25) property holds for t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N} then it also holds for t+1t+1 for each 𝒚∈ℝS\bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{S} as

(𝑩𝒅)t+1​𝒚=𝑩𝒅​(𝑩𝒅)t​𝒚≥clt​𝑩𝒅​(𝑷𝒅)t​𝒚l≥clt+1​𝑷𝒅​(𝑷𝒅)t​𝒚l=clt+1​(𝑷𝒅)t+1​𝒚l.\displaystyle(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})^{t+1}\bm{y}\;=\;\bm{B}^{\bm{d}}(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})^{t}\bm{y}\;\geq\;c_{\mathrm{l}}^{t}\bm{B}^{\bm{d}}(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{t}\bm{y}_{\mathrm{l}}\;\geq\;c_{\mathrm{l}}^{t+1}\bm{P}^{\bm{d}}(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{t}\bm{y}_{\mathrm{l}}\;=\;c_{\mathrm{l}}^{t+1}(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{t+1}\bm{y}_{\mathrm{l}}.

Above, the first inequality follows from Lemma 3.3.15 and the inductive assumption, and the second inequality follows from (3.25) by setting 𝒙=𝑷𝒅​𝒚\bm{x}=\bm{P}^{\bm{d}}\bm{y}. The right inequality in (3.25) follows analogously.

Exploiting the fact that 𝜼≥𝟎\bm{\eta}\geq\bm{0} and substituting 𝒚=𝒃𝒅\bm{y}=\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}, 𝒚l=cl⋅𝒑𝒅\bm{y}_{\mathrm{l}}=c_{\mathrm{l}}\cdot\bm{p}^{\bm{d}}, 𝒚u=cu⋅𝒑𝒅\bm{y}_{\mathrm{u}}=c_{\mathrm{u}}\cdot\bm{p}^{\bm{d}} into (3.25) and using the bounds in (3.24), we get that

0≤clt+1⋅𝜼⊤​(𝑷𝒅)t​𝒑𝒅≤𝜼⊤​(𝑩𝒅)t​𝒃𝒅≤cut+1⋅𝜼⊤​(𝑷𝒅)t​𝒑𝒅,\displaystyle 0\;\leq\;c_{\mathrm{l}}^{t+1}\cdot\bm{\eta}^{\top}(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{t}\bm{p}^{\bm{d}}\;\leq\;\bm{\eta}^{\top}(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})^{t}\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}\;\leq\;c_{\mathrm{u}}^{t+1}\cdot\bm{\eta}^{\top}(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{t}\bm{p}^{\bm{d}},

where the terms are non-negative because all constants, matrices, and vectors are non-negative. Therefore,

𝜼⊤(𝑩𝒅)t𝒃𝒅=0⇔𝜼⊤(𝑷𝒅)t𝒑𝒅=0.\bm{\eta}^{\top}(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})^{t}\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}=0\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\bm{\eta}^{\top}(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{t}\bm{p}^{\bm{d}}=0.

∎

Lemma 3.3.17.

For each π=(𝐝)∞∈ΠSR\pi=(\bm{d})_{\infty}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SR}}, there exists an 𝐟∈ℝS\bm{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{S} such that

𝒇⊤​𝑩𝒅=ρ⁡(𝑩𝒅)⋅𝒇⊤,𝒇≥𝟎,𝒇≠𝟎,𝒇⊤​𝒃𝒅>0.\bm{f}^{\top}\bm{B}^{\bm{d}}=\rho(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})\cdot\bm{f}^{\top},\quad\bm{f}\geq\bm{0},\quad\bm{f}\neq\bm{0},\quad\bm{f}^{\top}\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}>0.
Proof.

Because 𝑩𝒅\bm{B}^{\bm{d}} is non-negative, there exists an 𝒇∈ℝS\bm{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{S} from the Perron-Frobenius theorem (110, Theorem 8.3.1), such that

𝒇⊤​𝑩𝒅=ρ⁡(𝑩𝒅)⋅𝒇⊤,𝒇≥𝟎,𝒇≠𝟎.\bm{f}^{\top}\bm{B}^{\bm{d}}=\rho(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})\cdot\bm{f}^{\top},\qquad\bm{f}\geq\bm{0},\qquad\bm{f}\neq\bm{0}.

Furthermore, because 𝒃𝒅≥𝟎\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}\geq\bm{0}, we also have that

𝒇⊤​𝒃𝒅≥𝟎.\bm{f}^{\top}\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}\geq\bm{0}.

To prove the theorem, it remains to show that 𝒇⊤​𝒃𝒅≠0\bm{f}^{\top}\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}\neq 0, which we do by deriving a contradiction. Note that the 𝒇\bm{f} constructed from the Perron-Frobenius theorem is scale-independent. Therefore, without loss of generality, assume that 𝟏⊤​𝒇=1\bm{1}^{\top}\bm{f}=1 and suppose that 𝒇⊤​𝒃𝒅=0\bm{f}^{\top}\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}=0. Then:

𝒇⊤​𝒃𝒅\displaystyle\bm{f}^{\top}\bm{b}^{\bm{d}} =0\displaystyle=0
𝒇⊤​(𝑩𝒅)k​𝒃𝒅\displaystyle\bm{f}^{\top}(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})^{k}\bm{b}^{\bm{d}} =0,∀k∈ℕ\displaystyle=0,\,\forall k\in\mathbb{N} [ from ​𝒇⊤​𝑩𝒅=ρ⁡(𝑩𝒅)⋅𝒇⊤​]\displaystyle\text{[ from }\bm{f}^{\top}\bm{B}^{\bm{d}}=\rho(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})\cdot\bm{f}^{\top}\text{]}
𝒇⊤​(𝑷𝒅)k​𝒑𝒅\displaystyle\bm{f}^{\top}(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{k}\bm{p}^{\bm{d}} =0,∀k∈ℕ\displaystyle=0,\,\forall k\in\mathbb{N} [ from Lemma 3.3.16 ]
∑k=0t−1𝒇⊤​(𝑷𝒅)k​𝒑𝒅\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\bm{f}^{\top}(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{k}\bm{p}^{\bm{d}} =0,∀t∈ℕ,t>0\displaystyle=0,\,\forall t\in\mathbb{N},t>0 [ by summing elements ]
𝒇⊤​(𝑰−(𝑷𝒅)t)​𝟏\displaystyle\bm{f}^{\top}(\bm{I}-(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{t})\bm{1} =0,∀t∈ℕ\displaystyle=0,\,\forall t\in\mathbb{N} [ from Lemma 3.3.14 ]
limt→∞𝒇⊤​(𝑰−(𝑷𝒅)t)​𝟏\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}\bm{f}^{\top}(\bm{I}-(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{t})\bm{1} =0,\displaystyle=0, [ limit ]
𝒇⊤​𝟏\displaystyle\bm{f}^{\top}\bm{1} =0,\displaystyle=0, [ from Lemma 3.2.3 ]

which is a contradiction with 𝟏⊤​𝒇≠0\bm{1}^{\top}\bm{f}\neq 0. The last step in the derivation follows from ρ⁡(𝑷𝒅)<1\rho(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})<1 and therefore limt→∞(𝑷𝒅)t=𝟎\lim_{t\to\infty}(\bm{P}^{\bm{d}})^{t}=\bm{0} (4, Theorem 4.5). ∎

Proof of Lemma 3.3.13.

From Lemma 3.3.17, there exists an 𝒇∈ℝ+S\bm{f}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{S} that 𝒇⊤​𝑩𝒅=ρ⁡(𝑩𝒅)⋅𝒇⊤\bm{f}^{\top}\bm{B}^{\bm{d}}=\rho(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})\cdot\bm{f}^{\top} and 𝒇≥𝟎,𝒇≠𝟎\bm{f}\geq\bm{0},\bm{f}\neq\bm{0}. Then from (3.20):

−∞\displaystyle-\infty <𝜼⊤​𝒘t​(π,𝒛)\displaystyle<\bm{\eta}^{\top}\bm{w}^{t}(\pi,\bm{z})
=−𝜼⊤​(𝑩𝒅)t​𝒛−𝜼⊤​∑k=0t−1(𝑩𝒅)k​𝒃𝒅\displaystyle=-\bm{\eta}^{\top}(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})^{t}\bm{z}-\bm{\eta}^{\top}\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})^{k}\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}
≤−∑k=0t−1ρ(𝑩𝒅)k𝜼⊤𝒃𝒅.\displaystyle\leq-\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\rho(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})^{k}\bm{\eta}^{\top}\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}.

The second inequality follows because 𝒛≥𝟎\bm{z}\geq\bm{0} and 𝑩𝒅\bm{B}^{\bm{d}} is non-negative. Since 𝜼⊤​𝒃>0\bm{\eta}^{\top}\bm{b}>0 from Lemma 3.3.17, we can cancel it from the inequality getting that

∑k=0t−1ρ​(𝑩𝒅)k<∞.\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\rho(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})^{k}<\infty.

Then ρ⁡(𝑩𝒅)<1\rho(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})<1 because ρ⁡(𝑩𝒅)≥0\rho(\bm{B}^{\bm{d}})\geq 0 and the geometric series above is bounded. ∎

The limitation of Lemma 3.3.13 is that it only applies to stationary policies. The lemma does not preclude the possibility that all stationary policies have unbounded returns, but a Markov policy with a bounded return exists. We construct an upper bound on 𝒘t,⋆\bm{w}^{t,\star} that decreases monotonically in tt and converges to show this is impossible. The proof then concludes by squeezing 𝒘t,⋆\bm{w}^{t,\star} between the lower and the upper bound with the same limits. This technique allows us to relax the limiting assumptions from prior work [113, 60]. Finally, our results imply that an optimal stationary policy exists whenever the planning horizon TT is sufficiently large. Because the set ΠSD\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}} is finite, one policy must be optimal for a sufficiently large TT. This property suggests behavior similar to turnpikes in discounted MDPs [106].

3.3.3  Algorithms

We now briefly describe the algorithms we use to compute the optimal ERM-TRC policies. Surprisingly, the main algorithms for discounted MDPs, including value iteration, policy iteration, and linear programming, can be adapted to this risk-averse setting with only minor modifications.

Value iteration is the most direct method for computing the optimal value function [106]. The value iteration computes a sequence of 𝒘k,k=0,…\bm{w}^{k},k=0,\dots such that

𝒘k+1=L⋆​𝒘k,𝒘0=𝟎.\bm{w}^{k+1}=L^{\star}\bm{w}^{k},\quad\bm{w}^{0}=\bm{0}.

The initialization of 𝒘0=𝟎\bm{w}^{0}=\bm{0} is essential and guarantees convergence directly from the monotonicity argument used to prove Theorem 3.3.9.

Policy iteration (PI) starts by initializing with a stationary policy π0=(𝒅0)∞∈ΠSD\pi_{0}=(\bm{d}^{0})_{\infty}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}}. Then, for each iteration k=0,…k=0,\dots, PI alternates between the policy evaluation step and the policy improvement step:

𝒘k=−(𝑰−𝑩𝒅k)−1​𝒃𝒅k,𝒅k+1∈argmax𝒅∈𝒟𝑩𝒅​𝒘k−𝒃𝒅.\bm{w}^{k}=-(\bm{I}-\bm{B}^{\bm{d}^{k}})^{-1}\bm{b}^{\bm{d}^{k}},\;\bm{d}^{k+1}\in\argmax_{\bm{d}\in\mathcal{D}}\bm{B}^{\bm{d}}\bm{w}^{k}-\bm{b}^{\bm{d}}.

PI converges because it monotonically improves the value functions when initialized with a policy 𝒅0\bm{d}^{0} that has a bounded return [113]. However, we lack a practical approach to finding such an initial policy.

Finally, linear programming is a fast and convenient method for computing optimal exponential value functions:

min{𝟏⊤𝒘∣𝒘∈ℝS,𝒘≥−𝒃a+𝑩a𝒘,∀a∈𝒜}.\min\left\{\bm{1}^{\top}\bm{w}\mid\bm{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{S},\bm{w}\geq-\bm{b}^{a}+\bm{B}^{a}\bm{w},\,\forall a\in\mathcal{A}\right\}. (3.26)

Here, 𝑩s,⋅a=(Bs,s1a,⋯,Bs,sSa)\bm{B}_{s,\cdot}^{a}=(B_{s,s_{1}}^{a},\cdots,B_{s,s_{S}}^{a}), Bs,s′aB_{s,s^{\prime}}^{a} and bsab_{s}^{a} are constructed as in (3.14). We use the shorthand 𝑩a=𝑩𝒅\bm{B}^{a}=\bm{B}^{\bm{d}} and 𝒃a=𝒃𝒅\bm{b}^{a}=\bm{b}^{\bm{d}} where da′​(s)=1d_{a^{\prime}}(s)=1 if a=a′a=a^{\prime} for each s∈𝒮,a′∈𝒜s\in\mathcal{S},a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}.

It is important to note that the value functions, as well as the coefficients of 𝑩𝒅\bm{B}^{\bm{d}} may be irrational. It is, therefore, essential to study the sensitivity of the algorithms to errors in the input. However, this question is beyond the scope of the present paper, and we leave it for future work.

3.4  Solving EVaR Total Reward Criterion

This section shows that the EVaR-TRC objective can be reduced to a sequence of ERM-TRC problems, similarly to the discounted case [39]. As a result, an optimal stationary EVaR-TRC policy exists and can be computed using the methods described in Section 3.3.

Formally, we aim to compute a policy that maximizes the EVaR of the random return at some given fixed risk level α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) defined as

supπ∈ΠHRlim inft→∞EVaRαπ,𝝁⁡[∑k=0t−1r⁡(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)].\sup_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}}}\liminf_{t\to\infty}\evaro_{\alpha}^{\pi,\bm{\mu}}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right]. (3.27)

In contrast with [118], the objective in (3.27) optimizes EVaR rather than Nested EVaR.

3.4.1  Reduction to ERM-TRC

To solve (3.27), we exploit that EVaR can be defined in terms of ERM as shown in (4.2). To that end, define a function ht:ΠHR×ℝ→ℝ¯h_{t}\colon\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}}\times\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\bar{\mathbb{R}} for t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N} as

ht​(π,β):=gt​(π,β)+β−1​log⁡(α),h_{t}(\pi,\beta)\;:=\;g_{t}(\pi,\beta)+\beta^{-1}\log(\alpha), (3.28)

where gtg_{t} is the ERM value of the policy defined in (3.9). Also, ht⋆h_{t}^{\star}, h∞h_{\infty}, h∞⋆h_{\infty}^{\star} are defined analogously in terms of gt⋆g_{t}^{\star}, g∞g_{\infty}, and g∞⋆g_{\infty}^{\star} respectively. The functions hh are useful, because by (4.2):

EVaRαπ,𝝁​[∑k=0t−1r⁡(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)]=supβ>0ht​(π,β),\evaro_{\alpha}^{\pi,\bm{\mu}}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right]\;=\;\sup_{\beta>0}h_{t}(\pi,\beta), (3.29)

for each π∈ΠHR\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}} and t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}. However, note that the limit in the definition of supβ>0h∞⋆​(β)\sup_{\beta>0}h_{\infty}^{\star}(\beta) is inside the supremum, unlike in the objective in (3.27).

There are two challenges with solving (3.27) by reducing it to (3.29). First, the supremum in the definition of EVaR in (4.2) may not be attained, as mentioned previously. Second, the functions gt⋆g_{t}^{\star} and ht⋆h_{t}^{\star} may not converge uniformly to g∞⋆g_{\infty}^{\star} and h∞⋆h_{\infty}^{\star}. Note that Theorem 3.3.9 only shows pointwise convergence when the functions are bounded.

To circumvent the challenges described above, we replace the supremum in (3.29) with a maximum over a finite set ℬ⁡(β0,δ)\mathcal{B}(\beta_{0},\delta) of discretized β\beta values:

ℬ⁡(β0,δ):={β0,β1,…,βK},\mathcal{B}(\beta_{0},\delta)\;:=\;\left\{\beta_{0},\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{K}\right\}, (3.30a)
where δ>0\delta>0, 0<β0<β1<⋯<βK0<\beta_{0}<\beta_{1}<\dots<\beta_{K}, and
βk+1:=βk​log⁡1αlog⁡1α−βk​δ,βK≥log⁡1αδ,\beta_{k+1}\;:=\;\frac{\beta_{k}\log\frac{1}{\alpha}}{\log\frac{1}{\alpha}-\beta_{k}\delta},\qquad\beta_{K}\;\geq\;\frac{\log\frac{1}{\alpha}}{\delta}, (3.30b)

for an appropriately chosen value KK for each β0\beta_{0} and δ\delta. We assume that the denominator in the expression for βk+1\beta_{k+1} in Eq. 4.17b is positive; otherwise βk+1=∞\beta_{k+1}=\infty and βk\beta_{k} is sufficiently large.

The construction in (4.17) resembles equations (19) and (20) in [39] but differs in the choice of β0\beta_{0} because Hoeffding’s lemma does not readily bound the TRC criterion.

The following auxiliary Lemma 3.4.1, Lemma 3.4.2, Lemma 3.4.3 and Lemma 3.4.4 will be used to bound the approximation error of hh.

Lemma 3.4.1.

Suppose that f:ℝ+→ℝ¯f\colon\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\bar{\mathbb{R}} is non-increasing and 0<β00<\beta_{0}. Then:

supβ∈[0,β0)(f⁡(β)+β−1​log​α)−(f⁡(β0)+β0−1​log​α)\displaystyle\sup_{\beta\in[0,\beta_{0})}(f(\beta)+\beta^{-1}\log\alpha)-(f(\beta_{0})+\beta_{0}^{-1}\log\alpha) ≤f⁡(0)−f⁡(β0).\displaystyle\leq\;f(0)-f(\beta_{0}).
Proof.

Follows immediately from the fact that f⁡(β)≤f⁡(0),∀β≥0f(\beta)\leq f(0),\forall\beta\geq 0 and β−1​log⁡α⁡<0,∀β>​0\beta^{-1}\log\alpha<0,\forall\beta>0. ∎

Lemma 3.4.2.

Suppose that f:ℝ+→ℝ¯f\colon\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\bar{\mathbb{R}} is non-increasing and 0<βk<βk+10<\beta_{k}<\beta_{k+1}. Then:

supβ∈[βk,βk+1)(f⁡(β)+β−1​log​α)−(f⁡(βk)+βk−1​log​α)\displaystyle\sup_{\beta\in[\beta_{k},\beta_{k+1})}(f(\beta)+\beta^{-1}\log\alpha)-(f(\beta_{k})+\beta_{k}^{-1}\log\alpha) ≤(βk+1−1−βk−1)⋅log⁡α.\displaystyle\leq\;(\beta_{k+1}^{-1}-\beta_{k}^{-1})\cdot\log\alpha.
Proof.

The proof uses the same technique as Lemma D.5 from [39]. We restate the proof here for completeness.

Using the fact that ff is non-increasing and β↦β−1​log⁡α\beta\mapsto\beta^{-1}\log\alpha is increasing we get that:

supβ∈[βk,βk+1)(f⁡(β)+β−1⋅log⁡(α))−(f⁡(βk)+βk−1⋅log⁡α)\displaystyle\sup_{\beta\in[\beta_{k},\beta_{k+1})}\left(f(\beta)+\beta^{-1}\cdot\log(\alpha)\right)-\left(f(\beta_{k})+\beta_{k}^{-1}\cdot\log\alpha\right)
≤supβ∈[βk,βk+1)(f⁡(β)+βk+1−1⋅log⁡α)−(f⁡(βk)+βk−1⋅log⁡α)\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\beta\in[\beta_{k},\beta_{k+1})}\left(f(\beta)+\beta_{k+1}^{-1}\cdot\log\alpha\right)-\left(f(\beta_{k})+\beta_{k}^{-1}\cdot\log\alpha\right)
≤supβ∈[βk,βk+1)(f⁡(β)−f⁡(βk))+(βk+1−1⋅log⁡(α)−βk−1⋅log⁡α)\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\beta\in[\beta_{k},\beta_{k+1})}\left(f(\beta)-f(\beta_{k})\right)+\left(\beta_{k+1}^{-1}\cdot\log(\alpha)-\beta_{k}^{-1}\cdot\log\alpha\right)
≤βk+1−1⋅log⁡α−βk−1⋅log⁡α.\displaystyle\leq\beta_{k+1}^{-1}\cdot\log\alpha-\beta_{k}^{-1}\cdot\log\alpha.

∎

Lemma 3.4.3.

Suppose that f:ℝ+→ℝ¯f\colon\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\bar{\mathbb{R}} is non-increasing and 0<βK0<\beta_{K}. Then:

supβ∈[βK,∞)(f⁡(β)+β−1​log​α)−(f⁡(βK)+βK−1​log​α)≤−log⁡(α)βK.\displaystyle\sup_{\beta\in[\beta_{K},\infty)}(f(\beta)+\beta^{-1}\log\alpha)-(f(\beta_{K})+\beta_{K}^{-1}\log\alpha)\;\leq\;\frac{-\log(\alpha)}{\beta_{K}}.
Proof.

The proof uses the same technique as Lemma D.6 from [39]. We restate the proof here for completeness.

Because ff non-increasing and β−1⋅log⁡α≤0,∀β>0\beta^{-1}\cdot\log\alpha\leq 0,\forall\beta>0 we get that:

supβ∈[βK,∞)(f⁡(β)+β−1​log​α)−(f⁡(βK)+βK−1​log​α)≤supβ∈[βK,∞)(f⁡(β))−(f⁡(βK)+βK−1​log​α)≤−log⁡(α)βK.\displaystyle\sup_{\beta\in[\beta_{K},\infty)}(f(\beta)+\beta^{-1}\log\alpha)-(f(\beta_{K})+\beta_{K}^{-1}\log\alpha)\leq\sup_{\beta\in[\beta_{K},\infty)}(f(\beta))-(f(\beta_{K})+\beta_{K}^{-1}\log\alpha)\leq\frac{-\log(\alpha)}{\beta_{K}}.

∎

Lemma 3.4.4.

Suppose that f:ℝ+→ℝ¯f\colon\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\bar{\mathbb{R}} is non-increasing and ℬ⁡(β,δ)\mathcal{B}(\beta,\delta) defined in (4.17). Then for each β0>0\beta_{0}>0 and δ>0\delta>0:

maxβ∈ℬ⁡(β0,δ)⁡f⁡(β)+β−1​log⁡α\displaystyle\max_{\beta\in\mathcal{B}(\beta_{0},\delta)}f(\beta)+\beta^{-1}\log\alpha ≤supβ>0f⁡(β)+β−1​log⁡α\displaystyle\leq\;\sup_{\beta>0}f(\beta)+\beta^{-1}\log\alpha
≤maxβ∈ℬ⁡(β0,δ)⁡f⁡(β)+β−1​log⁡α+max⁡{f⁡(0)−f⁡(β0),δ}.\displaystyle\leq\;\max_{\beta\in\mathcal{B}(\beta_{0},\delta)}f(\beta)+\beta^{-1}\log\alpha+\max\left\{f(0)-f(\beta_{0}),\delta\right\}.

The result follows by algebraic manipulation from Lemmas 3.4.1, 3.4.2 and 3.4.3. ∎

Proposition 3.4.5.

Assume a given β0>0\beta_{0}>0 and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) such that β0​δ<log⁡1α\beta_{0}\delta<\log\frac{1}{\alpha}. Then, to satisfy the condition in (4.17b), it is sufficient to choose KK as

(11−z)K\displaystyle\left(\frac{1}{1-z}\right)^{K} ≥1z\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{z}
K\displaystyle K ≥log⁡zlog⁡(1−z),\displaystyle\geq\frac{\log z}{\log(1-z)},

since z∈(0,1)z\in(0,1) by the assumption β0​δ<log⁡1α\beta_{0}\delta<\log\frac{1}{\alpha}. ∎

The following theorem shows that one can obtain an optimal ERM policy for an appropriately chosen β\beta that approximates an optimal EVaR policy arbitrarily closely.

Theorem 3.4.6.

For any δ>0\delta>0, let

(π⋆,β⋆)∈argmax(π,β)∈ΠSD×ℬ⁡(β0,δ)h∞​(π,β),(\pi^{\star},\beta^{\star})\in\argmax_{(\pi,\beta)\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}}\times\mathcal{B}(\beta_{0},\delta)}h_{\infty}(\pi,\beta),

where β0>0\beta_{0}>0 is chosen such that g∞⋆​(0)≤g∞⋆​(β0)−δg_{\infty}^{\star}(0)\leq g_{\infty}^{\star}(\beta_{0})-\delta. Then the limits below exist and satisfy:

limt→∞EVaRαπ⋆,𝝁​[∑k=0t−1r⁡(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)]≥supπ∈ΠHRlimt→∞supβ>0ht​(π,β)−δ.\lim_{t\to\infty}\evaro_{\alpha}^{\pi^{\star},\bm{\mu}}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right]\geq\sup_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}}}\lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_{\beta>0}h_{t}(\pi,\beta)-\delta. (3.32)

Note that the right-hand side in (4.20) is the δ\delta-optimal objective in (3.27).

Proof of Theorem 4.3.6.

From Lemma 3.3.1, we can choose a β0>0\beta_{0}>0 be such that g∞⋆​(0)−g∞⋆​(β0)≤δg_{\infty}^{\star}(0)-g^{\star}_{\infty}(\beta_{0})\leq\delta.

Then we can upper bound the objective as:

supπ∈ΠHRlimt→∞supβ>0ht​(π,β)\displaystyle\sup_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}}}\lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_{\beta>0}h_{t}(\pi,\beta) ≤(a)limt→∞supβ>0supπ∈ΠHRht​(π,β)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(a)}}}{{\leq}}\lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_{\beta>0}\sup_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}}}h_{t}(\pi,\beta)
=(b)limt→∞supβ>0ht⋆​(β)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(b)}}}{{=}}\lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_{\beta>0}h_{t}^{\star}(\beta)
≤(c)limt→∞maxβ∈ℬ⁡(β0,δ)⁡ht⋆​(β)+δ\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(c)}}}{{\leq}}\lim_{t\to\infty}\max_{\beta\in\mathcal{B}(\beta_{0},\delta)}h_{t}^{\star}(\beta)+\delta
≤(d)max⁡limt→∞β∈ℬ⁡(β0,δ)⁡ht⋆​(β)+δ\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(d)}}}{{\leq}}\max_{\beta\in\mathcal{B}(\beta_{0},\delta)}\lim_{t\to\infty}h_{t}^{\star}(\beta)+\delta
