Let π⋆∈ΠSD,β⋆∈ℬ⁡(β0,δ)\pi^{\star}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}},\beta^{\star}\in\mathcal{B}(\beta_{0},\delta) be the maximizers that attain the objective above:

h∞​(π⋆,β⋆)=maxβ∈ℬ⁡(β0,δ)⁡h∞⋆​(β).h_{\infty}(\pi^{\star},\beta^{\star})=\max_{\beta\in\mathcal{B}(\beta_{0},\delta)}h_{\infty}^{\star}(\beta).

Then, continuing the upper bound on the objective:

maxβ∈ℬ⁡(β0,δ)⁡h∞⋆​(β)+δ\displaystyle\max_{\beta\in\mathcal{B}(\beta_{0},\delta)}h_{\infty}^{\star}(\beta)+\delta =h∞​(π⋆,β⋆)+δ\displaystyle=h_{\infty}(\pi^{\star},\beta^{\star})+\delta
=limt→∞ht​(π⋆,β⋆)+δ\displaystyle=\lim_{t\to\infty}h_{t}(\pi^{\star},\beta^{\star})+\delta
≤limt→∞supβ>0ht​(π⋆,β)+δ\displaystyle\leq\lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_{\beta>0}h_{t}(\pi^{\star},\beta)+\delta
≤limt→∞EVaRαπ⋆,𝝁⁡[∑k=0t−1r⁡(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)]+δ,\displaystyle\leq\lim_{t\to\infty}\evaro_{\alpha}^{\pi^{\star},\bm{\mu}}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right]+\delta,

which shows that π⋆\pi^{\star} is δ\delta-suboptimal since limt→∞EVaRαπ⋆,𝝁⁡[∑k=0t−1r⁡(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)]\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}\evaro_{\alpha}^{\pi^{\star},\bm{\mu}}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right] is a lower bound on the objective. ∎

The first implication of Theorem 4.3.6 is that there exists an optimal stationary deterministic policy.

Corollary 3.4.7.

There exists an optimal stationary deterministic policy π⋆∈ΠSD\pi^{\star}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}} that attains the supremum in (3.27).

Proof of Corollary 3.4.7.

Suppose that there exists a π^∈ΠHR∖ΠSD\hat{\pi}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{HR}}\setminus\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}} such that it attains an objective value greater than the best π∈ΠSD\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}} by at least ϵ>0\epsilon>0. Note that a best π∈ΠSD\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}} exists because ΠSD\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}} is finite. Then, one can derive a contradiction by choosing a π∈ΠSD\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}} that is at most ϵ/2\epsilon/2 suboptimal. ∎

The second implication of Theorem 4.3.6 is that it suggests an algorithm for computing the optimal, or near-optimal, stationary policy. We summarize it in Section 3.4.2.

3.4.2  Algorithms

We now propose a simple algorithm for computing a δ\delta-optimal EVaR policy described in Algorithm 4. The algorithm reduces finding optimal EVaR-TRC policies to solving a sequence of ERM-TRC problems in (3.8). As Theorem 4.3.6 shows, there exists a δ\delta-optimal policy such that it is ERM-TRC optimal for some β∈ℬ⁡(β0,δ)\beta\in\mathcal{B}(\beta_{0},\delta). It is, therefore, sufficient to compute an ERM-TRC optimal policy for one of those β\beta values.

The analysis above shows that Algorithm 4 is correct.

Corollary 3.4.8.

Algorithm 4 computes the δ\delta-optimal policy π⋆∈ΠSD\pi^{\star}\in\Pi_{\mathrm{SD}} that satifies the condition (4.20).

Corollary 3.4.8 follows directly from Theorem 4.3.6 and from the existence of a sufficiently small β0\beta_{0} from the continuity of g∞⋆​(β)g_{\infty}^{\star}(\beta) for positive β\beta around 00.

Algorithm 4 prioritizes simplicity over computational complexity and could be accelerated significantly. Evaluating each h∞⋆​(β)h_{\infty}^{\star}(\beta) requires computing an optimal ERM-TRC solution, which involves solving a linear program. One could reduce the number of evaluations of h∞⋆h_{\infty}^{\star} needed by employing a branch-and-bound strategy that takes advantage of the monotonicity of g∞⋆g_{\infty}^{\star}.

An additional advantage of Algorithm 4 is that the overhead of computing optimal solutions for multiple risk levels α\alpha can be small if one selects an appropriate set ℬ\mathcal{B}.

3.5  Numerical Evaluation

In this section, we illustrate our algorithms and formulations on tabular MDPs that include positive and negative rewards.

The ERM returns for the discounted and transient MDPs in Figure 3.1 with parameters r=−0.2,γ=0.9,ϵ=0.9r=-0.2,\,\gamma=0.9,\,\epsilon=0.9 are shown in Figure 3.2. The figure shows that, as expected, the returns are identical in the risk-neutral objective (when β=0\beta=0). However, for β>0\beta>0, the discounted and TRC returns differ significantly. The discounted return is unaffected by β\beta while the ERM-TRC return decreases with an increasing β\beta. Please see (67, appendix B) for more details.

To evaluate the effect of risk-aversion on the structure of the optimal policy, we use the gambler’s ruin problem [39, 43]. In this problem, a gambler starts with a given amount of capital and seeks to increase it up to a cap KK. In each turn, the gambler decides how much capital to bet. The bet doubles or is lost with a probability qq and 1−q1-q, respectively. The gambler can quit and retain their current wealth; the game also ends when the gambler goes broke or reaches the cap KK. The reward equals the final capital, except it is -1 when the gambler is broke. In the formulation, we use q=0.68q=0.68, and a cap is K=7K=7. The state space is 𝒮¯={0,1,⋯,7,e}\bar{\mathcal{S}}=\{0,1,\cdots,7,e\} and the action space is 𝒜={0,1,⋯,6}\mathcal{A}=\{0,1,\cdots,6\}. Action 00 represents quitting the game, and the other actions represent the bet size. The initial state is chosen randomly according to a uniform distribution over states 1,…,71,\dots,7. In state 00, the gambler has capital 00, takes the only available action 00, receives the reward −1-1, and transits to the sink state ee. That is: p¯​(0,0,e)=1\bar{p}(0,0,e)=1 and r¯​(0,0,e)=−1\bar{r}(0,0,e)=-1. If state 77, the gambler has capital 7, reaches the target wealth level, takes the only available action 00, receives the reward 77, and transits to the sink state ee. That is: p¯​(7,0,e)=1\bar{p}(7,0,e)=1 and r¯​(7,0,e)=7\bar{r}(7,0,e)=7. For the sink state ee, the only available action is 00, and the transition probabilities and rewards are p¯​(e,0,e)=1\bar{p}(e,0,e)=1 and r¯​(e,0,e)=0\bar{r}(e,0,e)=0. For other states s∈{1,…,6}s\in\left\{1,\dots,6\right\}, the gambler’s capital is ss, can take any action a∈{1,⋯,s}a\in\{1,\cdots,s\} to continue the game or an action 00 to quit the game. If the game is won, the gambler’s bet doubles. If the game is lost, the gambler’s bet is lost. That is, the transition probabilities and rewards for a∈{1,…,s}a\in\left\{1,\dots,s\right\} are

p¯​(s,a,s′)={qif ​s′=min⁡{s+a,7},1−qif ​s′=s−a,0otherwise,r¯​(s,a,s′)=0,\bar{p}(s,a,s^{\prime})=\begin{cases}q&\text{if }s^{\prime}=\min\left\{s+a,7\right\},\\ 1-q&\text{if }s^{\prime}=s-a,\\ 0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad\bar{r}(s,a,s^{\prime})=0,

for each s′∈{0,…,7,e}s^{\prime}\in\left\{0,\dots,7,e\right\} where q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1] is the win probability. If s∈{1,…,6}s\in\left\{1,\dots,6\right\} and the action is 00, the gambler quits the game and collects the reward. That is: p¯​(s,0,e)=1,\bar{p}(s,0,e)=1, and r¯​(s,0,e)=s\bar{r}(s,0,e)=s. The algorithm was implemented in Julia 1.10, and is available at https://github.com/suxh2019/ERMLP. Please see (67, appendix F) for more details.

Figure 3.3 shows optimal policies for four different EVaR risk levels α\alpha computed by Algorithm 4. The state represents the amount of capital the gambler holds. The optimal action indicates the amount of capital invested. The action zero means quitting the game. Note that there is only one action when the capital is 00 and 77 for all policies so that action is neglected in Figure 3.3. Since the optimal policy is stationary, we can interpret and analyze it effectively. The policies become notably less risk-averse as α\alpha increases. For example, when α=0.2\alpha=0.2, the gambler is very risk-averse and always quits with the current capital. When α=0.4\alpha=0.4, the gambler invests 11 when capital is greater than 11 and quits otherwise to avoid losing it all. When α=0.9\alpha=0.9, the gambler makes bigger bets, increasing the probability of reaching the cap and losing all capital.

To understand the impact of risk-aversion on the distribution of returns, we simulate the resulting policies over 7,000 episodes and show the distribution of capitals in Figure 3.4. When α=0.2\alpha=0.2, the return follows a uniform distribution on [1, 7]. When α=0.4\alpha=0.4, the returns are 11 and 77. When α=0.7\alpha=0.7 or 0.90.9, the returns are −1-1 and 77. Overall, the figure shows that for lower values of α\alpha, the gambler sacrifices some probability of reaching the cap in exchange for a lower probability of losing all their capital.

3.6  Conclusion and Future Work

We analyze transient MDPs with two risk measures: ERM and EVaR. We establish the existence of stationary deterministic optimal policies without any assumptions on the sign of the rewards, a significant departure from past work. Our results also provide algorithms based on value iteration, policy iteration, and linear programming for computing optimal policies.

Future directions include extensions to infinite-state TRC problems, risk-averse MDPs with average rewards, and partial-state observations.

CHAPTER 4Risk-Averse Total-Reward Reinforcement Learning

This chapter focuses on mitigating the effects of aleatoric uncertainty and risk due to the inherent stochasticity of the environment, without knowledge of the transition functions. The proposed Q-learning algorithms in this chapter belong to model-free RL approaches.

Risk-averse total-reward Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) offer a promising framework for modeling and solving undiscounted infinite-horizon objectives. Existing model-based algorithms for risk measures like the entropic risk measure (ERM) and entropic value-at-risk (EVaR) are effective in small problems, but require full access to transition probabilities. We propose a Q-learning algorithm to compute the optimal stationary policy for total-reward ERM and EVaR objectives with strong convergence and performance guarantees. The algorithm and its optimality are made possible by ERM’s dynamic consistency and elicitability. Our numerical results on tabular domains demonstrate quick and reliable convergence of the proposed Q-learning algorithm to the optimal risk-averse value function.

This work has been accepted by the 39th Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025). Xihong Su, Jia Lin Hau, Gersi Doko, Kishan Panaganti, Marek Petrik. Risk-Averse Total-Reward Reinforcement Learning (accepted). This work relates to Jia Lin Hau’s work [41], and he helped me better understand his paper. Jia and Gersi wrote the basic code to implement ERM and EVaR Q-learning algorithms. Kishan attended some meetings. Xihong wrote most of the code for this work and the draft. Marek and Xihong edited and finalized the paper.

4.1  Introduction

Risk-averse reinforcement learning (RL) is an essential framework for practical and high-stakes applications, such as self-driving, robotic surgery, healthcare, and finance [42, 61, 119, 41, 104, 120, 39, 68, 69, 33, 46, 44, 121, 122]. A risk-averse policy prefers actions with more certainty even if it means a lower expected return [29, 122]. The goal of Risk-averse RL is to compute risk-averse policies. To this end, RARL specifies the objective using monetary risk measures, such as value-at-risk (VaR), conditional-value-at-risk (CVaR), entropic risk measure (ERM), or entropic value at risk (EVaR). These risk measures penalize the variability of returns interpretably and yield policies with stronger guarantees on the probability of catastrophic losses [78].

A major challenge in deriving practical RL algorithms is that the model of the environment is often unknown. This challenge is even more salient in risk-averse RL because computing the risk of random return involves evaluating the full distribution of the return rather than just its expectation [41]. Traditional definitions of risk measures assume a known discounted [39, 68, 69, 33, 46, 44, 54] or transient [70] MDP model and use learning to approximate a global value or policy function [71]. Recent works have presented model-free methods to find optimal CVaR policies [73, 74] or optimal VaR policies [41], where the optimal policy may be Markovian or history-dependent. Another recent work derives a risk-sensitive Q-learning algorithm, which applies a nonlinear utility function to the temporal difference (TD) residual [29].

In RL domains formulated as Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), future rewards are handled differently based on whether the model is discounted or undiscounted. Most RL formulations assume discounted infinite-horizon objectives in which future rewards are assigned a lower value than present rewards. Discounting in financial domains is typically justified by interest rates and inflation, which make earlier rewards inherently more valuable [106, 123]. However, many RL tasks, such as robotics or games, have no natural justification for discounting. Instead, the domains have absorbing terminal states, which may represent desirable or undesirable outcomes [124, 125, 126].

Total reward criterion (TRC) generalizes stochastic shortest and longest path problems and has gained more attention [67, 70, 4, 61, 62, 63, 64, 31]. TRC has absorbing goal states and does not discount future rewards. A common assumption is that the MDP is transient and guarantees that any policy eventually terminates with positive probability. While this assumption is sufficient to guarantee finite risk-neutral expected returns, it is insufficient to guarantee finite returns with risk-averse objectives. For example, given an ERM objective, the risk level factor must also be sufficiently small to ensure a finite return [113, 70].

This paper derives risk-averse TRC model-free Q-learning algorithms for ERM-TRC and EVaR-TRC objectives. There are three main challenges to deriving these risk-averse TRC Q-learning algorithms. First, generalizing the standard Q-learning algorithm to risk-averse objectives requires computing the full return distribution rather than just its expectation. Second, the risk-averse TRC Bellman operator may not be a contraction. The absence of a contraction property precludes the direct application of model-free methods in an undiscounted MDP. Third, instead of relying on the contraction property, we need to utilize other properties of the Bellman operator and an additional bounded condition to prove the convergence of risk-averse TRC Q-learning algorithms.

As our main contribution,in this chapter, we prove that the ERM-TRC Q-learning algorithm and the EVaR-TRC Q-learning algorithm converge to the optimal risk-averse value functions. We also show that the proposed Q-learning algorithms compute the optimal stationary policies for the ERM and EVaR objectives, and the optimal state-action value function qq can be computed by the stochastic gradient descent along the derivative of the exponential loss function.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We define our research setting and preliminary concepts in Section 4.2. In Section 4.3, we leverage the elicitability of ERM, define a new ERM Bellman operator, and propose Q-learning algorithms for the ERM and EVaR objectives. In Section 4.4, we give a rigorous convergence proof of the proposed ERM-TRC Q-learning and EVaR-TRC Q-learning algorithms. Finally, the numerical results presented in Section 4.5 illustrate the effectiveness of our algorithms.

4.2  Preliminaries for Risk-aversion in Markov Decision Processes

We first introduce our notations and overview relevant properties for monetary risk measures. We then formalize the MDP framework with the risk-averse objective and summarize the standard Q-learning algorithm.

Notation

We denote by ℝ\mathbb{R} and ℕ\mathbb{N} the sets of real and natural (including 00) numbers, and ℝ¯:=ℝ∪{−∞,∞}\bar{\mathbb{R}}:=\mathbb{R}\cup\left\{-\infty,\infty\right\} denotes the extended real line. We use ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+} and ℝ+⁣+\mathbb{R}_{++} to denote non-negative and positive real numbers, respectively. We use a tilde to indicate a random variable, such as x~:Ω→ℝ\tilde{x}\colon\Omega\to\mathbb{R} for the sample space Ω\Omega. The set of all real-valued random variables is denoted as 𝕏:=ℝΩ\mathbb{X}:=\mathbb{R}^{\Omega}. Sets are denoted with calligraphic letters.

We defined monetary risk measures in previous chapters. Below we restate monetary risk measures for the convenience of readers.

Monetary risk measures

Monetary risk measures generalize the expectation operator to account for the uncertainty of the random variable. In this chapter, we focus on two risk measures. The first one is the entropic risk measure (ERM) defined for any risk level β>0\beta>0 and x~∈𝕏\tilde{x}\in\mathbb{X} as [78]

ERMβ[x~]:=−β−1⋅log𝔼exp(−β⋅x~),\displaystyle\ermo_{\beta}\left[\tilde{x}\right]\;:=\;-\beta^{-1}\cdot\log\mathbb{E}\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot\tilde{x}\right), (4.1)

and can be extended to β∈[0,∞]\beta\in[0,\infty] as ERM0⁡[x~]=limβ→0+ERMβ⁡[x~]=𝔼⁡[x~]\ermo_{0}[\tilde{x}]=\lim_{\beta\to 0^{+}}\ermo_{\beta}\left[\tilde{x}\right]=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{x}] and ERM∞[x~]=limβ→∞ERMβ[x~]=essinf[x~]\ermo_{\infty}[\tilde{x}]=\lim_{\beta\to\infty}\ermo_{\beta}\left[\tilde{x}\right]=\operatorname{ess}\inf[\tilde{x}]. ERM is popular because of its simplicity and its favorable properties in multi-stage optimization formulations [70, 39, 54, 41]. In particular, dynamic decision-making with ERM allows for the existence of dynamic programming equations and Markov or stationary optimal policies. In addition, in this work we leverage the fact that ERM is elicitable which means that it can be estimated by solving a linear regression problem [127, 128].

The second risk measure we consider is entropic value at risk (EVaR), which is defined for a given risk level α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and x~∈𝕏\tilde{x}\in\mathbb{X} as

EVaRα⁡[x~]\displaystyle\evaro_{\alpha}\left[\tilde{x}\right] :=supβ>0−β−1log(α−1𝔼exp(−βx~))=supβ>0ERMβ[x~]+β−1logα,\displaystyle:=\;\sup_{\beta>0}-\beta^{-1}\log\left(\alpha^{-1}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\tilde{x}\right)\right)\;=\;\sup_{\beta>0}\ermo_{\beta}\left[\tilde{x}\right]+\beta^{-1}\log\alpha, (4.2)

and is extended to EVaR0[x~]=essinf[x~]\evaro_{0}\left[\tilde{x}\right]=\ess\inf[\tilde{x}] and EVaR1⁡[x~]=𝔼⁡[x~]\evaro_{1}\left[\tilde{x}\right]=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{x}] [48]. It is important to note that the supremum in (4.2) may not be attained even when x~\tilde{x} is a finite discrete random variable [49]. EVaR addresses several important shortcomings of ERM [70, 39, 54, 41]. In particular, EVaR is coherent and closely approximates popular and interpretable quantile-based risk measures, like VaR and CVaR [48, 39].

Risk-Averse Markov Decision Processes

We formulate the decision process as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) (𝒮,𝒜,p,r,𝝁)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},p,r,\bm{\mu}) [106]. The set 𝒮={1,2,…,S,e}\mathcal{S}=\{1,2,\dots,S,e\} is the finite set of states and ee represents a sink state. The set 𝒜={1,2,…,A}\mathcal{A}=\{1,2,\ldots,A\} is the finite set of actions. The transition function p:𝒮×𝒜→Δ𝒮p\colon\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\Delta_{\mathcal{S}} represents the probability p⁡(s,a,s′)p(s,a,s^{\prime}) of transitioning to s′∈𝒮s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S} after taking a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} in s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}. The function r:𝒮×𝒜×𝒮→ℝr\colon\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R} represents the reward r⁡(s,a,s′)∈ℝr(s,a,s^{\prime})\in\mathbb{R} associated with transitioning from s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} and a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} to s′∈𝒮s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}. The vector 𝝁∈Δ𝒮\bm{\mu}\in\Delta_{\mathcal{S}} is the initial state distribution.

This chapter has the same objective as that in Chapter 3 and focus on computing stationary deterministic policies Π:=𝒜𝒮\Pi:=\mathcal{A}^{\mathcal{S}} that maximize the total reward criterion (TRC):

max⁡limt→∞π∈Π⁡Riskπ,𝝁⁡[∑k=0t−1r⁡(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)],\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\lim_{t\to\infty}\operatorname{Risk}^{\pi,\bm{\mu}}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right], (4.3)

where Risk represents either ERM or EVaR risk measures. The limit in (4.3) exists for stationary policies π\pi but may be infinite [70]. The superscript π\pi indicates the policy that guides the actions’ probability, and the 𝝁\bm{\mu} indicates the distribution over the initial states.

Recent work has shown that an optimal policy in (4.3) exists, is stationary, and has bounded return for a sufficiently small β\beta as long as the following assumptions hold [70]. The sink state ee satisfies that p⁡(e,a,e)=1p(e,a,e)=1 and r⁡(e,a,e)=0r(e,a,e)=0 for each a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, and μe=0\mu_{e}=0 [70]. It is crucial to assume that the MDP is transient for any π∈Π\pi\in\Pi:

∑t=0∞ℙπ,s[s~t=s′]<∞,∀s,s′∈𝒮∖{e}.\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}^{\pi,s}\left[\tilde{s}_{t}=s^{\prime}\right]\;<\;\infty,\qquad\forall s,s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}\setminus\left\{e\right\}. (4.4)

Intuitively, this assumption states that any policy eventually reaches the sink state and effectively terminates. We adopt these assumptions in the remainder of the paper.

With a risk-neutral objective, transient MDPs guarantee that the return is bounded for each policy. However, that is no longer the case with the ERM objective. In particular, for some β\beta it is possible that the return is unbounded. The return is bounded for a sufficiently small β\beta and there exists an optimal stationary policy [70]. In contrast, the return of EVaR is always bounded, and an optimal stationary policy always exists regardless of the risk level α\alpha [70].

Standard Q-learning

To help with the exposition of our new algorithms, we now informally summarize the Q-learning algorithm for a risk-neutral setting [125]. Q-learning is an essential component of most model-free reinforcement learning algorithms, including DQN and many actor-critic methods [129, 130, 131]. Its simplicity and scalability make it especially appealing.

Q-learning iteratively refines an estimate of the optimal state-action value function q~i:𝒮×𝒜→ℝ,i∈ℕ\tilde{q}_{i}\colon\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R},i\in\mathbb{N} such that it satisfies

q~i+1​(s~i,a~i)=q~i​(s~i,a~i)−η~i​z~i,z~i=r⁡(s~i,a~i,s~i′)+maxa′∈𝒜⁡q~i​(s~i,a′)−q~i​(s~i,a~i).\tilde{q}_{i+1}(\tilde{s}_{i},\tilde{a}_{i})=\tilde{q}_{i}(\tilde{s}_{i},\tilde{a}_{i})-\tilde{\eta}_{i}\tilde{z}_{i},\quad\tilde{z}_{i}=r(\tilde{s}_{i},\tilde{a}_{i},\tilde{s}^{\prime}_{i})+\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\tilde{q}_{i}(\tilde{s}_{i},a^{\prime})-\tilde{q}_{i}(\tilde{s}_{i},\tilde{a}_{i}). (4.5)

Here, z~i\tilde{z}_{i} is also known as the TD residual. The algorithm assumes a stream of samples (s~i,a~i,s~i′)i=1,…(\tilde{s}_{i},\tilde{a}_{i},\tilde{s}^{\prime}_{i})_{i=1,\dots} sampled from the transition probabilities and appropriately chosen step sizes η~i\tilde{\eta}_{i} to converge to the optimal state-action value function. Note that q~i\tilde{q}_{i} is random because it is a function of a random variable. It is well-known that the standard Q-learning algorithm can be seen as a stochastic gradient descent on the quadratic loss function [41, 132, 29]. We leverage this property to build our algorithms.

4.3  Q-learning Algorithms: ERM and EVaR

In this section, we derive new Q-learning algorithms for the ERM and EVaR objectives. First, we propose the Q-learning algorithm for ERM in Section 4.3.1, which requires us to introduce a new ERM Bellman operator based on the elicitability of the ERM risk measure. Then, we use this algorithm in Section 4.3.2 to propose an EVaR Q-learning algorithm.

4.3.1  ERM Q-learning Algorithm

The algorithm we propose in this section computes the state-action function for multiple values of the risk level β∈ℬ\beta\in\mathcal{B} for some given non-empty finite set ℬ⊆ℝ+⁣+\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{++} of positive reals. The set ℬ\mathcal{B} may be a singleton or may include multiple values, which is necessary to optimize EVaR in the next section.

Before describing the Q-learning algorithm, we define the ERM risk-averse state-action value function and describe the Bellman operator that can be used to compute it. We define the ERM risk-averse state-action value function qβ:𝒮×𝒜×ℬ→ℝ¯q_{\beta}\colon\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{B}\to\bar{\mathbb{R}} for each β∈ℬ\beta\in\mathcal{B} as

qπ​(s,a,β):=limt→∞ERMβπ,⟨s,a⟩​[∑k=0t−1r⁡(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)],q⋆​(s,a,β):=maxπ∈Π⁡qπ​(s,a,β).q^{\pi}(s,a,\beta):=\lim_{t\to\infty}\ermo_{\beta}^{\pi,\langle s,a\rangle}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right],\quad q^{\star}(s,a,\beta):=\max_{\pi\in\Pi}q^{\pi}(s,a,\beta). (4.6)

for each s∈𝒮,a∈𝒜,β∈ℬs\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A},\beta\in\mathcal{B}. The limit in this equation exists by (67, lemma D.5).

The superscript ⟨s,a⟩\left<s,a\right> in (4.6) indicates the initial state and action are s~0=s,a~0=a\tilde{s}_{0}=s,\tilde{a}_{0}=a, and the policy π\pi determines the actions henceforth. We use 𝒬:=ℝ𝒮×𝒜\mathcal{Q}:=\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}} to denote the set of possible state-action value functions.

To facilitate the computation of the value functions, we define the following ERM Bellman operator Bβ:ℝ𝒮×𝒜→ℝ𝒮×𝒜B_{\beta}\colon\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}}\to\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}} as

(Bβ​q)​(s,a):=ERMβa,s​[r⁡(s,a,s~1)+maxa′∈𝒜⁡q⁡(s~1,a′)],∀s∈𝒮,a∈𝒜,β∈ℬ,q∈𝒬.(B_{\beta}q)(s,a):=\ermo^{a,s}_{\beta}\left[r(s,a,\tilde{s}_{1})+\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}q(\tilde{s}_{1},a^{\prime})\right],\qquad\forall s\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A},\beta\in\mathcal{B},q\in\mathcal{Q}. (4.7)

Note that the Bellman operator BβB_{\beta} applies to the value functions q⁡(⋅,⋅,β)q(\cdot,\cdot,\beta) for a fixed value of β\beta. We abbreviate BβB_{\beta} to BB when the risk level β\beta is clear from the context.

The following result, which follows from (70, theorem 3.3), shows that the ERM state-action value function can be computed as the fixed point of the Bellman operator.

Theorem 4.3.1.

Assume some β∈ℬ\beta\in\mathcal{B} and suppose that qβ⋆​(s,a)>−∞,∀s∈𝒮,a∈𝒜q_{\beta}^{\star}(s,a)>-\infty,\forall s\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A}. Then qβ⋆q_{\beta}^{\star} in (4.6) is the unique solution to

qβ⋆=Bβ​qβ⋆,whereqβ⋆=q⋆​(⋅,⋅,β).q_{\beta}^{\star}\;=\;B_{\beta}q_{\beta}^{\star},\quad\text{where}\quad q^{\star}_{\beta}=q^{\star}(\cdot,\cdot,\beta). (4.8)
Proof.

The exponential value function w⋆​(s)w^{\star}(s) is the unique solution to the exponential Bellman equation (70, theorem 3.3). Therefore, for a state s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} and the optimal policy π\pi, state value function vπ​(s)v^{\pi}(s), and the exponential state value function wπ​(s)w^{\pi}(s), β∈ℬ\beta\in\mathcal{B}, we have that

vπ​(s)=−β−1​log⁡(−wπ​(s))v^{\pi}(s)=-\beta^{-1}\log(-w^{\pi}(s)) (4.9)

Because of the bijection between w⋆​(s)w^{\star}(s) and v⋆​(s)v^{\star}(s), we can conclude that v⋆​(s)v^{\star}(s) is the unique solution to the regular Bellman equation.

The optimal state value function can be rewritten in terms of the optimal state-action value function in (4.10)

v⋆​(s)=maxa′∈𝒜⁡q⋆​(s,a,β)v^{\star}(s)=\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}q^{\star}(s,a,\beta) (4.10)

Then q⋆​(s,a,β)q^{\star}(s,a,\beta) exists. The value q⋆q^{\star} is unique directly from the uniqueness of v⋆v^{\star}. ∎

Although the Bellman operator defined in (4.8) can be used to compute the value function when the transition probabilities are known, it is inconvenient in the model-free reinforcement learning setting where the state-action value function must be estimated directly from samples.

We now turn to an alternative definition of the Bellman operator that can be used to estimate the value function directly from samples. To develop our ERM Q-learning algorithm, we need to define a Bellman operator that is amenable to compute its fixed point using stochastic gradient descent. For this purpose, we use the elicitability property of risk measures [127]. ERM is known to be elicitable using the following loss function ℓβ:ℝ→ℝ\ell_{\beta}\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}:

ℓβ(z):=β−1(exp(−β⋅z)−1)+z,ℓβ′(z)=1−exp(−β⋅z),ℓβ′′(z)=β⋅exp(−β⋅z).\ell_{\beta}(z):=\beta^{-1}(\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot z\right)-1)+z,\quad\ell_{\beta}^{\prime}(z)=1-\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot z\right),\quad\ell_{\beta}^{\prime\prime}(z)=\beta\cdot\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot z\right). (4.11)

The functions ℓ′\ell^{\prime} and ℓ′′\ell^{\prime\prime} are the first and second derivatives which are be important in constructing and analyzing the Q-learning algorithm.

The following proposition summarizes the elicitability property of ERM, which we need to develop our Q-learning algorithm. Elicitable risk measures can be estimated using regression from samples in a model-free way.

Proposition 4.3.2.

For each x~∈𝕏\tilde{x}\in\mathbb{X} and β>0\beta>0:

ERMβ⁡[x~]=argminy∈ℝ𝔼​[ℓβ​(x~−y)],\ermo_{\beta}\left[\tilde{x}\right]=\argmin_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{E}[\ell_{\beta}(\tilde{x}-y)], (4.12)

where the minimum is unique because ℓβ\ell_{\beta} is strictly convex.

Proof.

The proof is broken into two parts. First, we show that ℓβ​(x~−y)\ell_{\beta}(\tilde{x}-y) is strictly convex, and a minimum value of ℓβ\ell_{\beta} exists. Second, we show that the minimizer of 𝔼​[ℓβ​(x~−y)]\mathbb{E}[\ell_{\beta}(\tilde{x}-y)] is equal to ERMβ⁡[x~]\ermo_{\beta}\left[\tilde{x}\right].

Take the first derivative of ℓβ​(x~−y)\ell_{\beta}(\tilde{x}-y) with respect to yy.

ℓβ​(x~−y)\displaystyle\ell_{\beta}(\tilde{x}-y) =β−1(e−β⋅(x~−y)−1)+(x~−y)\displaystyle=\beta^{-1}(e^{-\beta\cdot(\tilde{x}-y)}-1)+(\tilde{x}-y) (4.13)
ℓβ′​(y)\displaystyle\ell_{\beta}^{\prime}(y) =β−1(e−β⋅(x~−y))⋅β−1\displaystyle=\beta^{-1}(e^{-\beta\cdot(\tilde{x}-y)})\cdot\beta-1
ℓβ′​(y)\displaystyle\ell_{\beta}^{\prime}(y) =e−β⋅(x~−y)−1\displaystyle=e^{-\beta\cdot(\tilde{x}-y)}-1

Take the second derivative of ℓβ​(x~−y)\ell_{\beta}(\tilde{x}-y) with respect to yy

∂2ℓβ∂y2\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}\ell_{\beta}}{\partial y^{2}} =∂(e−β⋅(x~−y)−1)∂y\displaystyle=\frac{\partial(e^{-\beta\cdot(\tilde{x}-y)}-1)}{\partial y} (4.14)
ℓβ′′​(y)\displaystyle\ell_{\beta}^{\prime\prime}(y) =e−β⋅(x~−y)⋅β\displaystyle=e^{-\beta\cdot(\tilde{x}-y)}\cdot\beta
ℓβ′′​(y)\displaystyle\ell_{\beta}^{\prime\prime}(y) =βe−β⋅(x~−y)>0\displaystyle=\beta e^{-\beta\cdot(\tilde{x}-y)}>0

Therefore, ℓβ\ell_{\beta} is strongly convex with respect to yy, and the minimum value of ℓβ\ell_{\beta} exists.

Second, take the first derivative of 𝔼​[ℓβ​(x~−y)]\mathbb{E}[\ell_{\beta}(\tilde{x}-y)] with respective to yy

∂𝔼[β−1(e−β⋅(x~−y)−1)+(x~−y)]∂y\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathbb{E}\bigl[\beta^{-1}(e^{-\beta\cdot(\tilde{x}-y)}-1)+(\tilde{x}-y)\bigr]}{\partial y} =0\displaystyle=0
𝔼[e−β⋅(x~−y)−1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\beta\cdot(\tilde{x}-y)}-1\bigr] =0\displaystyle=0
𝔼[e−β⋅(x~−y)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\beta\cdot(\tilde{x}-y)}\bigr] =1\displaystyle=1
𝔼[e−β⋅x~]⋅𝔼[eβ⋅y]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\beta\cdot\tilde{x}}\bigr]\cdot\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\beta\cdot y}\bigr] =1\displaystyle=1
𝔼[e−β⋅x~]⋅eβ⋅y\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\beta\cdot\tilde{x}}\bigr]\cdot e^{\beta\cdot y} =1\displaystyle=1
e−β⋅y\displaystyle e^{-\beta\cdot y} =𝔼[e−β⋅x~]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\beta\cdot\tilde{x}}\bigr]
y\displaystyle y =−β−1log(𝔼[e−β⋅x~])\displaystyle=-\beta^{-1}\log(\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{-\beta\cdot\tilde{x}}\bigr])

Therefore, the minimizer of 𝔼​[ℓβ​(x~−y)]\mathbb{E}[\ell_{\beta}(\tilde{x}-y)] is equal to ERMβ⁡[x~]\ermo_{\beta}\left[\tilde{x}\right]. ∎

Using the elicitability property, we define the Bellman operator B^β:𝒬→𝒬\hat{B}_{\beta}\colon\mathcal{Q}\to\mathcal{Q} for β∈ℬ\beta\in\mathcal{B} as

(B^β​q)​(s,a):=argminy∈ℝ𝔼a,s​[ℓβ​(r⁡(s,a,s~1)+maxa′∈𝒜⁡q⁡(s~1,a′)−y)],∀s∈𝒮,a∈𝒜.(\hat{B}_{\beta}q)(s,a):=\argmin_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{E}^{a,s}\left[\ell_{\beta}\left(r(s,a,\tilde{s}_{1})+\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}q(\tilde{s}_{1},a^{\prime})-y\right)\right],\;\forall s\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A}. (4.15)

Following Proposition 4.3.2, we get the following equivalence of the Bellman operator, which implies that their fixed points coincide.

Theorem 4.3.3.

For each β>0\beta>0 and q∈𝒬q\in\mathcal{Q}, we have that

Bβ​q=B^β​q.B_{\beta}q=\hat{B}_{\beta}q.

We can introduce the ERM Q-learning algorithm in Algorithm 5 using the results above. This algorithm adapts the standard Q-learning approach to the risk-averse setting. Intuitively, it works as follows. Each iteration ii processes a single transition sample to update the optimal state-action value function estimate q~i\tilde{q}_{i}. The value function estimates are random because the samples are random. The value function estimates are updated following a stochastic gradient descent along the derivative of the loss function ℓβ\ell_{\beta} defined in (4.11). Each sample is used to simultaneously update the state-action value function for multiple values of β∈ℬ\beta\in\mathcal{B}.

There are three main differences between Algorithm 5 and the standard Q-learning algorithm described in Section 4.2. First, standard Q-learning aims to maximize the expectation objective, and the proposed algorithm maximizes the ERM-TRC objective. Second, the state-action value function update follows a sequence of stochastic gradient steps, but it replaces the quadratic loss function with the exponential loss function ℓβ\ell_{\beta} in (4.11). Third, qq values in the proposed algorithm need an additional bounded condition that the TD residual z~i​(β)\tilde{z}_{i}(\beta) is in [zmin,zmax][z_{\min},z_{\max}].

Remark 4.3.4.

The qq value can be unbounded for two main reasons. First, as the value of β\beta increases, the ERM value function does not increase (39, Lemma A.7) and can reach −∞-\infty (70, Theorem 3.3). Second, the agent has some probability of repeatedly receiving a reward for the same action, leading to an uncontrolled increase in the qq value for that action.

Note that if z~i​(β)\tilde{z}_{i}(\beta) is outside the [zmin,zmax][z_{\min},z_{\max}] range, it indicates that the value of the risk level β\beta is so large that q~\tilde{q} is unbounded. This aligns with the conclusion that the value function may be unbounded for a large risk factor [70, 113]. Detecting unbounded values of qq caused by random chance is useful but is challenging and beyond the scope of this work.

zmin​(β)=−2​max​{|c−β⋅d|,|c|}−‖r‖∞,zmax​(β)=2​max​{|c−β⋅d|,|c|}+‖r‖∞.z_{\min}(\beta)=-2\max\{|c-\beta\cdot d|,|c|\}-\|r\|_{\infty},\quad z_{\max}(\beta)=2\max\{|c-\beta\cdot d|,|c|\}+\|r\|_{\infty}.

4.3.2  EVaR Q-learning Algorithm

In this section, we adapt our ERM Q-learning algorithm to compute the optimal policy for the static EVaR-TRC objective in (4.3). As mentioned in Section 4.2, EVaR is preferable to ERM because it is coherent and closely approximates VaR and CVaR. The construction of an optimal EVaR policy follows the standard methodology proposed in prior work [70, 39]. We only briefly summarize it here.

The main challenge in solving (4.3) is that EVaR is not dynamically consistent, and the supremum in (4.2) may not be attained. We show that the EVaR-TRC problem can be reduced to a sequence of ERM-TRC problems, similarly to the discounted case [39] and the undiscounted case [70]. We define the objective function h:Π×ℝ+⁣+→ℝ¯h\colon\Pi\times\mathbb{R}_{++}\to\bar{\mathbb{R}}:

h⁡(π,β)\displaystyle h(\pi,\beta) :=ERMβπ,μ​[qπ​(s~0,a~0,β)]+β−1​log⁡(α)\displaystyle:=\;\ermo_{\beta}^{\pi,\mu}\left[q^{\pi}(\tilde{s}_{0},\tilde{a}_{0},\beta)\right]+\beta^{-1}\log(\alpha) (4.16)
=limt→∞ERMβπ,μ⁡[∑k=0t−1r⁡(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)]+β−1​log⁡(α).\displaystyle=\;\lim_{t\to\infty}\ermo_{\beta}^{\pi,\mu}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right]+\beta^{-1}\log(\alpha).

Recall that s~0\tilde{s}_{0} is distributed according to the initial distribution μ\mu and a~0\tilde{a}_{0} is the action distributed according to the policy π\pi. The equality in the equation above follows directly from the definition of the value function in (4.6).

We now compute a δ\delta-optimal EVaR-TRC policy for any δ>0\delta>0 by solving a sequence of ERM-TRC problems. Following prior work [70], we replace the supremum over continuous β\beta in the definition of EVaR in (4.2) with a maximum over a finite set ℬ⁡(β0,δ)\mathcal{B}(\beta_{0},\delta) of discretized β\beta values chosen as

ℬ⁡(β0,δ):={β0,β1,…,βK},\mathcal{B}(\beta_{0},\delta)\;:=\;\left\{\beta_{0},\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{K}\right\}, (4.17a)
where 0<β0<β1<⋯<βK0<\beta_{0}<\beta_{1}<\dots<\beta_{K}, and
βk+1:=βk​log⁡1αlog⁡1α−βk​δ,βK≥log⁡1αδ,K≥log⁡(θ)log⁡(1−θ),\beta_{k+1}\;:=\;\frac{\beta_{k}\log\frac{1}{\alpha}}{\log\frac{1}{\alpha}-\beta_{k}\delta},\quad\beta_{K}\;\geq\;\frac{\log\frac{1}{\alpha}}{\delta},\quad K\;\geq\;\frac{\log(\theta)}{\log(1-\theta)}, (4.17b)

for θ:=−β0⋅δ/log⁡(α)\theta:=-\nicefrac{{\beta_{0}\cdot\delta}}{{\log(\alpha)}}, and the minimal KK that satisfies the inequality. Note that the construction in (4.17) differs in the choice of β0\beta_{0} from ℬ⁡(β0,δ)\mathcal{B}(\beta_{0},\delta) in [39].

Let us derive β0\beta_{0}. For a desired precision δ>0\delta>0, β0\beta_{0} is chosen such that

𝔼π⋆,𝝁​[x~]−ERMβ0π⋆,𝝁​[x~]≤δ\mathbb{E}^{\pi^{\star},\bm{\mu}}[\tilde{x}]-\ermo_{\beta_{0}}^{\pi^{\star},\bm{\mu}}\left[\tilde{x}\right]\leq\delta (4.18)

For a random variable x~\tilde{x} and β>0\beta>0 (39, Lemma A.8)

𝔼⁡[x~]−ERMβ⁡[x~]≤β⋅(xmax−xmin)2/8\mathbb{E}[\tilde{x}]-\ermo_{\beta}\left[\tilde{x}\right]\leq\beta\cdot(x_{\max}-x_{\min})^{2}/8

Then we have

𝔼π⋆,𝝁​[x~]−ERMβ0π⋆,𝝁​[x~]≤β0⋅(xmax−xmin)2/8\mathbb{E}^{\pi^{\star},\bm{\mu}}[\tilde{x}]-\ermo_{\beta_{0}}^{\pi^{\star},\bm{\mu}}\left[\tilde{x}\right]\leq\beta_{0}\cdot(x_{\max}-x_{\min})^{2}/8 (4.19)

When the equality conditions in (4.18) and (4.19) hold, we have

β0⋅(xmax−xmin)2/8\displaystyle\beta_{0}\cdot(x_{\max}-x_{\min})^{2}/8 =δ\displaystyle=\delta
β0\displaystyle\beta_{0} =8​δ(xmax−xmin)2\displaystyle=\frac{8\delta}{(x_{\max}-x_{\min})^{2}}

where xmaxx_{\max} and xminx_{\min} are estimated in Algorithm 6.

The following theorem summarizes the fact that the EVaR-TRC problem reduces to a sequence of ERM-TRC optimization problems.

Theorem 4.3.6 (Theorem 4.2 in [67]).

For any δ>0\delta>0 and a sufficiently small β0>0\beta_{0}>0, let

(π⋆,β⋆)∈argmax(π,β)∈Π×ℬ⁡(β0,δ)h​(π,β).(\pi^{\star},\,\beta^{\star})\in\argmax_{(\pi,\beta)\in\Pi\times\mathcal{B}(\beta_{0},\delta)}h(\pi,\beta).

Then, the limits below exist and satisfy that

limt→∞EVaRαπ⋆,𝝁⁡[∑k=0t−1r⁡(s~k,a~k,s~k+1)]≥supπ∈Πlimt→∞supβ>0h⁡(π,β)−δ.\lim_{t\to\infty}\evaro_{\alpha}^{\pi^{\star},\bm{\mu}}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}r(\tilde{s}_{k},\tilde{a}_{k},\tilde{s}_{k+1})\right]\;\geq\;\sup_{\pi\in\Pi}\lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_{\beta>0}h(\pi,\beta)-\delta. (4.20)

Algorithm 7 summarizes the procedure for computing a δ\delta-optimal EVaR policy. Note that the value of h⁡(π,β)h(\pi,\beta) may be −∞-\infty, indicating either the ERM-TRC objective is unbounded for β\beta, or the Q-learning algorithm diverged by random chance.

Remark 4.3.7.

Note that Algorithm 7 assumes a small β0\beta_{0} as its input. It is unclear whether it is possible to obtain a prior bound on β0\beta_{0} without knowing the model. We, therefore, employ the heuristic outlined in Algorithm 6 that estimates a lower bound xminx_{\min} and an upper bound xmaxx_{\max} on the random variable of returns. Then, we set β0:=8​δ/(xmax−xmin)2.\beta_{0}:=\nicefrac{{8\delta}}{{(x_{\max}-x_{\min})^{2}}}.

4.4  Convergence Analysis

This section presents our main convergence guarantees for the ERM-TRC Q-learning and EVaR-TRC Q-learning algorithms.

We require the following standard assumption to prove the convergence of the proposed Q-learning algorithms. The intuition of Assumption 4.4.1 is that each state-action pair must be visited infinitely often.

Assumption 4.4.1.

The input to Algorithm 5 and Algorithm 7 satisfies that

ℙ[s~i′=s′∣𝒢i−1,s~i,a~i,η~i]=p(s~i,a~i,s′),∀s′∈𝒮,∀i∈ℕ,\mathbb{P}[\tilde{s}^{\prime}_{i}=s^{\prime}\mid\mathcal{G}_{i-1},\tilde{s}_{i},\tilde{a}_{i},\tilde{\eta}_{i}]=p(\tilde{s}_{i},\tilde{a}_{i},s^{\prime}),\qquad\forall s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S},\,\forall i\in\mathbb{N},

almost surely, where 𝒢i−1:=(η~l,(sl~,a~l,s~l′))l=0i−1\mathcal{G}_{i-1}:=(\tilde{\eta}_{l},(\tilde{s_{l}},\tilde{a}_{l},\tilde{s}^{\prime}_{l}))_{l=0}^{i-1}.

The following theorem shows that the proposed ERM-TRC Q-learning algorithm enjoys convergence guarantees comparable to standard Q-learning. As Remark 4.3.5 states, zminz_{\min} and zmaxz_{\max} are chosen to ensure that qq values are bounded.

Theorem 4.4.2.

For β∈ℬ\beta\in\mathcal{B}, assume that the sequence (η~i)i=0∞\left(\tilde{\eta}_{i}\right)_{i=0}^{\infty} and ((,,,,,))i=0∞\left((\tilde{s}_{i},\tilde{a}_{i},\tilde{s}^{\prime}_{i})\right)_{i=0}^{\infty} used in Algorithm 5 satisfies Assumption 4.4.1 and step size condition

∑i=0∞η~i=∞,∑i=0∞η~i2<∞,\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\tilde{\eta}_{i}=\infty,\quad\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\tilde{\eta}_{i}^{2}<\infty,

where i∈{i∈ℕ∣(s~i,a~i)=(s,a)}i\in\{i\in\mathbb{N}\mid(\tilde{s}_{i},\tilde{a}_{i})=(s,a)\}, if z~i∈[zmin,zmax]\tilde{z}_{i}\in[z_{\min},z_{\max}] almost surely, then the sequence (q~i)i=0∞(\tilde{q}_{i})_{i=0}^{\infty} produced by Algorithm 5 convergences almost surely to q∞q_{\infty} such that q∞=B^β​q∞q_{\infty}=\hat{B}_{\beta}q_{\infty}.

The proof of Theorem 4.4.2 follows an approach similar to that in the proofs of standard Q-learning [133] with three main differences. First, the algorithm converges for an undiscounted MDP, and B^\hat{B} is not a contraction captured by (133, assumption 4.4), which is restated here as Assumption A.1.2. Instead, we show that B^\hat{B} satisfies monotonicity in Lemma 4.4.3. Second, Assumption A.1.2 leads to a convergence result somewhat weaker than the results for a contraction. Then, a separate boundedness condition(133, proposition 4.6) is imposed. Third, using exponential loss function ℓβ\ell_{\beta} requires a more careful choice of step-size than the standard analysis. The proof of Theorem 4.4.2 is shown in Section A.2.

Lemma 4.4.3.

For β∈ℬ\beta\in\mathcal{B}, let 𝟏∈ℝn\bm{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} represent the vector of all ones. Then the ERM Bellman operator defined in (4.15) satisfies the monotonicity property if for some g>0g>0 and q⋆:ℝ𝒮×𝒜→ℝ𝒮×𝒜q^{\star}\colon\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}}\to\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}} and for all q:ℝ𝒮×𝒜→ℝ𝒮×𝒜q\colon\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}}\to\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}} it satisfies that

x≤y\displaystyle x\leq y ⇒B^β​x≤B^β​y\displaystyle\quad\Rightarrow\quad\hat{B}_{\beta}x\leq\hat{B}_{\beta}y (a)
B^β​q⋆\displaystyle\hat{B}_{\beta}q^{\star} =q⋆\displaystyle\quad=\quad q^{\star} (b)
B^β​q−g⋅𝟏≤B^β​(q−g⋅𝟏)\displaystyle\hat{B}_{\beta}q-g\cdot\bm{1}\quad\leq\quad\hat{B}_{\beta}(q-g\cdot\bm{1}) ≤B^β​(q+g⋅𝟏)≤B^β​q+g⋅𝟏\displaystyle\quad\leq\quad\hat{B}_{\beta}(q+g\cdot\bm{1})\quad\leq\quad\hat{B}_{\beta}q+g\cdot\bm{1} (c)

Here, the relations hold element-wise.

Proof.

First, from Theorem 4.3.3, we have

Bβ​q\displaystyle B_{\beta}q =B^β​q\displaystyle=\hat{B}_{\beta}q
⇓\displaystyle\Downarrow
ERMβa,s⁡[r⁡(s,a,s~1)+maxa′∈𝒜⁡q⁡(s~1,a′,β)]\displaystyle\ermo^{a,s}_{\beta}\Bigl[r(s,a,\tilde{s}_{1})+\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}q(\tilde{s}_{1},a^{\prime},\beta)\Bigr] =argminy∈ℝ𝔼a,s​[ℓβ​(r⁡(s,a,s~1)+maxa′∈𝒜⁡q⁡(s~1,a′,β)−y)]\displaystyle=\argmin_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{E}^{a,s}\Bigl[\ell_{\beta}\bigl(r(s,a,\tilde{s}_{1})+\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}q(\tilde{s}_{1},a^{\prime},\beta)-y\bigr)\Bigr]

For the part (a)(a), ERM is monotone [39]. That is, for some fixed β∈ℬ\beta\in\mathcal{B} value, if x≤yx\leq y, then B^β​x≤B^β​y\hat{B}_{\beta}x\leq\hat{B}_{\beta}y.

For the part (b)(b), ℓβ\ell_{\beta} is a strongly convex function because ℓβ′′(y)=β⋅e−β⋅(x~−y)>0\ell^{\prime\prime}_{\beta}(y)=\beta\cdot e^{-\beta\cdot(\tilde{x}-y)}>0. Then there will be a unique y⋆y^{\star} value such that 𝔼a,s​[ℓβ​(r⁡(s,a,s~1)+maxa′∈𝒜⁡q⁡(s~1,a′,β)−y)]\mathbb{E}^{a,s}\Bigl[\ell_{\beta}\bigl(r(s,a,\tilde{s}_{1})+\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}q(\tilde{s}_{1},a^{\prime},\beta)-y\bigr)\Bigr] attains the minimum value, and the y⋆y^{\star} value is equal to q⋆​(s,a,β)q^{\star}(s,a,\beta), which follows from Proposition 4.3.2. So B^β​q⋆=q⋆\hat{B}_{\beta}q^{\star}=q^{\star}

For the part (c)(c), ERM is monotone and satisfies the law-invariance property [39].

B^β​(q)−1⋅g≤(1)B^β​(q−1⋅g)≤(2)B^β​(q+1⋅g)≤(3)B^β​(q)+1⋅g\displaystyle\hat{B}_{\beta}(q)-1\cdot g\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(1)}}}{{\leq}}\hat{B}_{\beta}(q-1\cdot g)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(2)}}}{{\leq}}\hat{B}_{\beta}(q+1\cdot g)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(3)}}}{{\leq}}\hat{B}_{\beta}(q)+1\cdot g

Steps (1)(1) and (3)(3) follow from the law-invariance property of ERM. Step (2)(2) follows from the mononotone property of ERM. ∎

The following lemma shows that the loss function lβl_{\beta} is strongly convex and has a Lipschitz-continuous gradient. These properties are instrumental in showing the uniqueness of our value functions and analyzing the convergence of our Q-learning algorithms by analyzing them as a form of stochastic gradient descent.

Lemma 4.4.4.

The function ℓβ:[zmin,zmax]→ℝ\ell_{\beta}\colon[z_{\min},z_{\max}]\to\mathbb{R} defined in (4.11) is ll-strongly convex with l=βexp(−β⋅zmax)l=\beta\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot z_{\max}\right) and its derivative ℓβ′​(z)\ell_{\beta}^{\prime}(z) is LL-Lipschitz-continuous with L=β⋅exp(−β⋅zmin)L=\beta\cdot\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta\cdot z_{\min}\right).

Proof.

We use the fact that ℓβ\ell_{\beta} is twice continuously differentiable and prove the ll-strong convexity from (134, theorem 2.1.11):

l=infz∈[zmin,zmax]ℓβ′′​(z)=infz∈[zmin,zmax]β​exp⁡(−β​z)=β​exp⁡(−β​zmax).l=\inf_{z\in[z_{\min},z_{\max}]}\ell_{\beta}^{\prime\prime}(z)=\inf_{z\in[z_{\min},z_{\max}]}\beta\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta z\right)=\beta\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta z_{\max}\right).

To prove LL-Lipschitz continuity of the derivative, using (135, Theorem 9.7), we have that

L=supz∈[zmin,zmax]|ℓβ′′​(z)|=supz∈[zmin,zmax]|β​exp⁡(−β​z)|=β​exp⁡(−β​zmin).L=\sup_{z\in[z_{\min},z_{\max}]}|\ell_{\beta}^{\prime\prime}(z)|=\sup_{z\in[z_{\min},z_{\max}]}|\beta\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta z\right)|=\beta\operatorname{exp}\left(-\beta z_{\min}\right).

∎

Corollary 4.4.5, which follows immediately from Theorem 4.3.6, shows that Algorithm 7 enjoys convergence guarantees and converges to a δ\delta-optimal EVaR policy.

Corollary 4.4.5.

For α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and δ>0\delta>0, assume that the sequence {η~i}i=0∞\{\tilde{\eta}_{i}\}_{i=0}^{\infty} and {(s~i,a~i,s~i′)}i=0∞\{(\tilde{s}_{i},\tilde{a}_{i},\tilde{s}^{\prime}_{i})\}_{i=0}^{\infty} used in Algorithm 5 satisfies Assumption 4.4.1 and step size condition

∑i=0∞η~i=∞,∑i=0∞η~i2<∞,\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\tilde{\eta}_{i}=\infty,\quad\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\tilde{\eta}_{i}^{2}<\infty,

where i∈{i∈ℕ∣(s~i,a~i)=(s,a)}i\in\{i\in\mathbb{N}\mid(\tilde{s}_{i},\tilde{a}_{i})=(s,a)\}, if z~i∈[zmin,zmax]\tilde{z}_{i}\in[z_{\min},z_{\max}]. Then Algorithm 7 converges to the δ\delta-optimal stationary policy π⋆\pi^{\star} for the EVaR-TRC objective in (4.3) almost surely.

The proof of Corollary 4.4.5 follows a similar approach to the proofs of Theorem 4.4.2. However, we also need to show that one can obtain an optimal ERM policy for an appropriately chosen β\beta that approximates an optimal EVaR policy arbitrarily closely.

Proof.

From Theorem 4.4.2, for some β∈ℬ\beta\in\mathcal{B}, the ERM-Q learning algorithm converges to the optimal ERM value function. Theorem 4.3.6 shows that there exists δ−\delta-optimal policy such that it is an ERM-TRC optimal for some β∈ℬ\beta\in\mathcal{B}. It is sufficient to compute an ERM-TRC optimal policy for one of those β\beta values. This analysis shows that Algorithm 7 converges to its optimal EVaR value function. ∎

4.5  Numerical Evaluation

In this section, we evaluate our algorithms on two tabular domains: cliff walking (CW) [125] and gambler’s ruin (GR) [70].

First, to evaluate our EVaR Q-learning algorithm with risk levels α=0.2\alpha=0.2 and α=0.6\alpha=0.6, we use the cliff walk problem. In this problem, an agent starts with a random state (cell in the grid world) that is uniformly distributed over all non-sink states and walks toward the goal state labeled by gg shown in Figure 4.2. At each step, the agent takes one of four actions: up, down, left, or right. The action will be performed with a probability of 0.910.91, and the other three actions will also be performed separately with a probability of 0.030.03. If the agent hits the wall, it will stay in its place. The reward is zero in all transitions except for the states marked with cc, dd, and gg. The agent receives 22 in state gg, 0.0040.004 in state dd, and −0.5,−0.6,−0.7,−0.8-0.5,-0.6,-0.7,-0.8, or −0.9-0.9 in cliff region marked with cc from the left to the right. If an agent steps into the cliff region, it will immediately be returned to the state marked with bb. Note that the agent has unlimited steps, and the future rewards are not discounted.

Before computing the optimal EVaR policy, we set βc=1−10\beta_{c}=1^{-10} in Algorithm 6 to compute cc and dd in Remark 4.3.5. cc and dd are used to estimate the bounds of z~i​(β)\tilde{z}_{i}(\beta) in ERM-TRC Q-learning algorithm. Figure 4.2 shows the optimal policy for EVaR risk level α=0.2\alpha=0.2 computed by Algorithm 7. Each cell represents a state, and the arrow direction indicates the optimal action to take in that state. Note that the optimal actions for states cc and gg are the same and are omitted in Figure 4.2 and Figure 4.2. Since the optimal policy is stationary, it can be interpreted and analyzed visually. The agent moves right to the last column of the grid world and then moves down to reach the goal. When the agent is close to the cliff region, it moves up to avoid risk. Figure 4.2 shows the optimal policy for EVaR risk level α=0.6\alpha=0.6 computed by Algorithm 7. Different optimal actions are highlighted in blue. As we can see, for different risk levels α\alpha, when the agent is near the cliff region, it exhibits consistent behaviors to avoid falling off the cliff. For the remaining states, the agent behaves differently.

Second, to understand the impact of risk aversion on the structure of returns, we simulate the two optimal EVaR policies over 48,00048,000 episodes and display the distribution of returns in Figure 4.4. The xx-axis represents the possible return the agent can get for each episode, and the yy-axis represents the percentage of getting a certain amount of return over 48,00048,000 episodes. The start state is uniformly distributed over all states except the goal. For each episode, the agent starts with a non-sink state, takes 20,00020,000 steps, and collects all rewards during the path. When α=0.6\alpha=0.6, the return is in (−1,2](-1,2], and its mean value is −0.074-0.074, and its standard deviation is 0.2280.228. When α=0.2\alpha=0.2, the return is in (0,2](0,2], its mean value is 1.921.92, and its standard deviation is 0.2280.228. Overall, Figure 4.4 shows that for the lower value of α\alpha, the agent has a higher probability of avoiding falling off the cliff.

Third, to assess the stability of our EVaR-TRC Q-learning algorithm, we use six random seeds to generate samples, compute the optimal policies, and calculate the EVaR values on the CW domain. In Figure 4.4, the risk level α\alpha is 0.30.3, and the yy axis represents the mean value and standard deviation of the EVaR values calculated in samples generated by six random seeds. Figure 4.4 shows that our Q-learning algorithm converges to similar solutions across different numbers of samples. The standard deviation is 0.0210.021. Note that our Q-learning algorithm could converge to a different optimal EVaR policy depending on the learning rate and the number of samples.

Finally, we evaluate the convergence of Algorithm 7, which approximates the EVaR value calculated from the linear programming(LP) [70] on CW and GR domains. The CW domain has one absorbing terminal state, and the GR domain has two absorbing terminal states. The xx axis represents the number of samples, and the yy axis represents the difference in EVaR values computed by LP and Q-learning algorithms. In Figure 4.6, the risk level α\alpha is 0.40.4, and the EVaR value difference decreases to zero when the number of samples is around 20,000 on the CW domain. In Figure 4.6, the risk level α\alpha is 0.30.3, and the EVaR value difference decreases to zero when the number of samples is around 30,000 on the GR domain. We illustrate the convergence result for some α\alpha values, but the conclusion applies to any α\alpha value. Overall, our Q-learning algorithm converges to the optimal value function.

4.6  Conclusion and Limitations

In this chapter, we proposed two new risk-averse model-free algorithms for risk-averse reinforcement learning objectives. We also proved the convergence of the proposed algorithm under mild assumptions. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first risk-averse model-free algorithms for the TRC criterion. Studying the TRC criterion in risk-averse RL is essential because it exhibits dramatically different properties in risk-averse objectives compared to the discounted criterion.

An important limitation of this work is that our algorithms focus on the tabular setting and do not analyze the impact of value function approximation. However, the work lays out solid foundations for building approximately scalable reinforcement learning algorithms. In particular, a strength of Q-learning is that it can be coupled with general value function approximation schemes, such as deep neural networks. Although extending convergence guarantees to such approximate settings is challenging, our convergence results show that our Q-learning algorithm is a sound foundation for scalable, practical algorithms. Future work should include a rigorous numerical evaluation of the deep learning implementation of the Q-learning algorithms.

Our theoretical analysis has two main limitations that may preclude its use in some practical settings. First, we must choose the limits zmin,zmaxz_{\min},z_{\max}. If these limits are set too small, the algorithms may fail to compute a good solution, and if they are too large, the algorithms may be excessively slow to detect the divergence of the TRC criterion for large values of β\beta. The second limitation is the need to select the parameter β0\beta_{0} that guarantees the existence of a δ\delta-optimal EVaR solution. A natural choice for β0\beta_{0} was proposed in [70], but it requires several runs of Q-learning just to establish an appropriate β0\beta_{0}. Future work needs to develop a better methodology for establishing these parameters. However, it is unclear whether a proper model-free solution is possible without making additional assumptions about the structure of the MDP.

CHAPTER 5Conclusion

Researchers are actively working and have achieved some success in mitigating the effects of uncertainty and risk in sequential decision-making applications, such as self-driving cars, robotic surgery, healthcare, and finance. However, designing algorithms that are deployed to effectively mitigate the effects of uncertainty and risk in critical and high-stakes applications is still a challenging task. In this dissertation, we propose several efficient algorithms to mitigate the effects of uncertainty and risk in sequential decision-making processes. The optimal polices computed by the proposed algorithms are easy to interpret and deploy in real-world scenarios.

First, we proposed the CADP algorithm to guarantee that it never performs worse than previous dynamic programming algorithms, such as WSU. WSU has no guarantee of the optimality of its computed policy. CADP takes the coordinate ascent perspective to adjust model weights iteratively to guarantee monotone policy improvements to a local maximum. Our numerical results indicate that CADP substantially outperforms existing methods on several benchmark problems. Note that the objective is to find a Markov policy that maximizes the discounted return averaged over an MMDP. The discounted criterion is a very common choice in MDPs, especially for infinite-horizon problems. Also, the discount factor ensures that the Bellman equations satisfy the contraction property (used for dynamic programming), and the value functions are always bounded. The limitation of this work is that the state space and action space are finite. Future work should adapt this approach to deep reinforcement learning and use neural networks to approximate weights.

Second, we focus on the total reward criterion under ERM and EVaR risk measures and propose exponential value iteration, policy iteration, and linear programming algorithms to compute the optimal stationary policies for the risk-averse TRC objectives. Unlike the discounted criterion, the Bellman operator in TRC may not be a contraction, and the value functions can be unbounded. We establish the sufficient and necessary conditions for the Bellman operator to be a contraction. The experiment is based on the tabular Gambler domain. Our results indicate that the total reward criterion may be preferable to the discounted criterion in a broad range of risk-averse reinforcement learning domains. Future work will evaluate the proposed algorithm on various benchmarks and practical problems. Future directions include extensions to infinite-state TRC problems, risk-averse MDPs with average rewards, and partial-state observations.

Third, to address the unknown model of the environment, such as critical and high-stakes applications in practice, we proposed Q-learning algorithms to compute the optimal stationary policy for total-reward ERM and EVaR objectives. Because the transition dynamic is unknown, the contraction conditions of the ERM Bellman operator do not apply to this case. Instead, we use the monotonicity of the ERM Bellman operator to prove the convergence of risk-averse Q-learning algorithms. Our numerical results on the Gabmber ruin and cliff walking domains demonstrate quick and reliable convergence of the proposed Q-learning algorithm to the optimal risk-averse value function computed by linear programming. This work lays out solid foundations for building scalable approximation reinforcement learning algorithms. In particular, a strength of Q-learning is that it can be coupled with general value function approximation schemes, such as deep neural networks. Future work should include rigorous numerical evaluation of deep learning implementation of the Q-learning algorithms. Additionally, future work can investigate other learning rate methods and regularization techniques to mitigate the impact of the learning rate and the number of samples in Q-learning.

Overall, we investigate the discounted criterion under an expectation objective for an MMDP and the total reward criterion under risk-averse objectives for an MDP. We develop several efficient model-based and model-free algorithms to compute the optimal policies for these objectives. We believe that these approaches open up many opportunities to gain a deeper understanding of the fundamental issues involved in a broad range of risk-averse discounted-reward and total-reward reinforcement learning domains.

Appendix A

A.1  Standard Convergence Results

Our convergence analysis of Q-learning algorithms is guided by the framework [133, section 4]. We summarize the framework in this section. Consider the following iteration for some random sequence r~i:Ω→ℝ𝒩\tilde{r}_{i}:\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{N}} where 𝒩={1,2,⋯,n}\mathcal{N}=\{1,2,\cdots,n\}, then Q-learning is defined as

r~i+1​(b)\displaystyle\tilde{r}_{i+1}(b) =(1−θ~i(b))⋅r~i(b)+θ~i(b)⋅((Hr~i)(b)+ϕ~i(b)),i=0,1,⋯\displaystyle=(1-\tilde{\theta}_{i}(b))\cdot\tilde{r}_{i}(b)+\tilde{\theta}_{i}(b)\cdot((H\tilde{r}_{i})(b)+\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)),\quad i=0,1,\cdots (A.1)
=r~i(b)+θ~i(b)⋅((Hr~i)(b)+ϕ~i(b)−r~i(b)),i=0,1,⋯\displaystyle=\tilde{r}_{i}(b)+\tilde{\theta}_{i}(b)\cdot((H\tilde{r}_{i})(b)+\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)-\tilde{r}_{i}(b)),\quad i=0,1,\cdots

for all b∈𝒩b\in\mathcal{N}, where H:ℝ𝒩→ℝ𝒩H:\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{N}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{N}}is some possibly non-linear operator, θ~i:Ω→ℝ+⁣+\tilde{\theta}_{i}:\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{++} is a step size, and ϕ~i:Ω→ℝ𝒩\tilde{\phi}_{i}:\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{N}} is some random noise sequence. The random history ℱi\mathcal{F}_{i} at iteration i=1,⋯i=1,\cdots is denoted by

ℱi=(r~0,⋯,r~i,ϕ~0,⋯,ϕ~i−1,θ~0,⋯,θ~i).\mathcal{F}_{i}=(\tilde{r}_{0},\cdots,\tilde{r}_{i},\tilde{\phi}_{0},\cdots,\tilde{\phi}_{i-1},\tilde{\theta}_{0},\cdots,\tilde{\theta}_{i}).

The following assumptions will be needed to analyze and prove the convergence of our algorithms.

Assumption A.1.1.

[assumption 4.3 in [133]]

  1. (a)

    For every ii and bb, we have

    𝔼​[ϕ~​(b)|ℱi]=0\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}(b)|\mathcal{F}_{i}]=0
  2. (b)

    There exists a norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| on ℝ𝒩\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{N}} and constants AA and BB such that

    𝔼⁡[ϕ~i​(b)2|ℱi]≤A+B​‖r~i‖2\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)^{2}|\mathcal{F}_{i}]\leq A+B\|\tilde{r}_{i}\|^{2}
Assumption A.1.2.

[assumption 4.4 in [133]]

  1. (a)

    The mapping HH is monotone: that is, if r≤r¯r\leq\bar{r}, then H​r≤H​r¯Hr\leq H\bar{r}.

  2. (b)

    There exists a unique vector r⋆r^{\star} satisfying H​r⋆=r⋆Hr^{\star}=r^{\star}.

  3. (c)

    If e∈ℝne\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the vector with all components equal to 1, and if η\eta is a positive scalar, then

    H​r−η⋅e≤H⁡(r−η⋅e)≤H⁡(r+η⋅e)≤H​r+η⋅eHr-\eta\cdot e\leq H(r-\eta\cdot e)\leq H(r+\eta\cdot e)\leq Hr+\eta\cdot e

Note that Assumption A.1.2 leads to a convergence result somewhat weaker than the results for weighted maximum norm pseudo-contraction. Then we need a separate boundedness condition [133, proposition 4.6], which is restated here as Proposition A.1.3.

Proposition A.1.3 (proposition 4.6 in [133]).

Let rtr_{t} be the sequence generated by the iteration shown in Eq. A.1. We assume that the bbth component r~​(b)\tilde{r}(b) of r~\tilde{r} is updated according to Eq. A.1, with the understanding that θ~i​(b)=0\tilde{\theta}_{i}(b)=0 if r~​(b)\tilde{r}(b) is not updated at iteration ii. ϕ~i​(b)\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b) is a random noise term. Then we assume the following:

  1. (a)

    The step sizes θ~i​(b)\tilde{\theta}_{i}(b) are nonnegative and satisfy

    ∑i=0∞θ~i​(b)=∞,∑i=0∞θ~i2​(b)<∞,\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\tilde{\theta}_{i}(b)=\infty,\quad\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\tilde{\theta}_{i}^{2}(b)<\infty,
  2. (b)

    The noise terms ϕ~i​(b)\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b) satisfies Assumption A.1.1,

  3. (c)

    The mapping HH satisfies Assumption A.1.2.

If the sequence r~i\tilde{r}_{i} is bounded with probability 1, then r~i\tilde{r}_{i} converges to r⋆r^{\star} with probability 1.

A.2  Proof of Theorem 4.4.2

To prove Theorem 4.4.2, we need to define some operators and analyze their properties, and prove the properties of random noise.

(H​q)​(b):=q⁡(b)−ξ⋅(G​q)​(b),(Hs′​q)​(b):=q⁡(b)−ξ⋅(Gs′​q)​(b)(Hq)(b):=q(b)-\xi\cdot(Gq)(b),\qquad(H_{s^{\prime}}q)(b):=q(b)-\xi\cdot(G_{s^{\prime}}q)(b) (A.4)

ϕ~i​(s,a,β)={(Hs~i​q~i)​(s,a)−(H​q~i)​(s,a),if ​(s~i,a~i)=(s,a)0,otherwise \tilde{\phi}_{i}(s,a,\beta)=\begin{cases}(H_{\tilde{s}_{i}}\tilde{q}_{i})(s,a)-(H\tilde{q}_{i})(s,a),&\text{if }(\tilde{s}_{i},\tilde{a}_{i})=(s,a)\\ 0,&\text{otherwise }\\ \end{cases} (A.5)

The random sequences of iterations followed by Algorithm 5 satisfies

Let us restate [41, C.13] as Lemma A.2.2, which is useful to prove that the operator HH satisfies monotonicity.

Lemma A.2.2 (C.13 in [41]).

Suppose that f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is a differentiable μ−\mu-strongly convex function with an L−L-Lipschitz continuous gradient. Consider xi∈ℝx_{i}\in\mathbb{R} and a gradient update for any step size ξ∈(0,1/L]:\xi\in(0,1/L]:

xi+1:=xi−ξ⋅f′​(xi)x_{i+1}:=x_{i}-\xi\cdot f^{\prime}(x_{i})

Then ∃l∈[1/L,1/μ]\exists l\in[1/L,1/\mu] such that ξ/l∈(0,1]\xi/l\in(0,1] and

xi+1=(1−ξ/l)⋅xi+ξ/l⋅x⋆x_{i+1}=(1-\xi/l)\cdot x_{i}+\xi/l\cdot x^{\star}

where x⋆=argminx∈ℝf​(x)x^{\star}=\argmin_{x\in\mathbb{R}}f(x) (unique from strong convexity)

Lemma A.2.3.

(H​q⋆)​(b)\displaystyle(Hq^{\star})(b) =q⋆​(b)\displaystyle=q^{\star}(b) (b)
(H​q)​(b)−𝟏⋅g≤H⁡(q⁡(b)−𝟏⋅g)\displaystyle(Hq)(b)-\bm{1}\cdot g\leq H(q(b)-\bm{1}\cdot g) ≤H⁡(q⁡(b)+𝟏⋅g)≤(H​q)​(b)+𝟏⋅g.\displaystyle\leq H(q(b)+\bm{1}\cdot g)\leq(Hq)(b)+\bm{1}\cdot g. (c)

First, we prove part (a)(a): fix β>0\beta>0 and some b=(s,a,β),s∈𝒮,a∈𝒜b=(s,a,\beta),s\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A}. Fix qq and define

=(a)q⁡(b)−ξ​f′​(q⁡(b))\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(a)}}}{{=}}q(b)-\xi f^{\prime}(q(b))

=\displaystyle= (1−ξ/l)⋅q−(1−ξ/l)⋅c⋅e+(ξ/l)⋅B^​q−(ξ/l)⋅c⋅e\displaystyle(1-\xi/l)\cdot q-(1-\xi/l)\cdot c\cdot e+(\xi/l)\cdot\hat{B}q-(\xi/l)\cdot c\cdot e
=\displaystyle= (1−ξ/l)​(q−c⋅e)+(ξ/l)​(B^​q−c⋅e)\displaystyle(1-\xi/l)(q-c\cdot e)+(\xi/l)(\hat{B}q-c\cdot e)
=(a)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(a)}}}{{=}} (1−ξ/l)​(q−c⋅e)+(ξ/l)​(B^​(q−c⋅e))\displaystyle(1-\xi/l)(q-c\cdot e)+(\xi/l)(\hat{B}(q-c\cdot e))
=\displaystyle= H⁡(q−c⋅e)\displaystyle H(q-c\cdot e)

Step (a)(a) follows from the law invariance property of ERM [39].

2) Let us prove H⁡(q−c⋅e)≤H⁡(q+c⋅e)H(q-c\cdot e)\leq H(q+c\cdot e)

Because q−c⋅e≤q+c⋅eq-c\cdot e\leq q+c\cdot e and the part (a)(a) of the operator HH, we have

H⁡(q−c⋅e)≤H⁡(q+c⋅e)H(q-c\cdot e)\leq H(q+c\cdot e)

3) Let us prove H⁡(q+c⋅e)=H⁡(q)+c⋅eH(q+c\cdot e)=H(q)+c\cdot e

H⁡(q+c⋅e)\displaystyle H(q+c\cdot e)
=\displaystyle= (1−ξ/l)​(q+c⋅e)+(ξ/l)​B^​(q+c⋅e)\displaystyle(1-\xi/l)(q+c\cdot e)+(\xi/l)\hat{B}(q+c\cdot e)
=\displaystyle= (1−ξ/l)​(q+c⋅e)+(ξ/l)​(B^​(q)+c⋅e)\displaystyle(1-\xi/l)(q+c\cdot e)+(\xi/l)(\hat{B}(q)+c\cdot e)
=(a)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(a)}}}{{=}} (1−ξ/l)​(q+c⋅e)+(ξ/l)​B^​(q)+(ξ/l)⋅c⋅e\displaystyle(1-\xi/l)(q+c\cdot e)+(\xi/l)\hat{B}(q)+(\xi/l)\cdot c\cdot e
=\displaystyle= (1−ξ/l)​q+(1−ξ/l)⋅(c⋅e)+(ξ/l)⋅c⋅e+(ξ/l)​B^​(q)\displaystyle(1-\xi/l)q+(1-\xi/l)\cdot(c\cdot e)+(\xi/l)\cdot c\cdot e+(\xi/l)\hat{B}(q)
=\displaystyle= (1−ξ/l)​q+c⋅e+(ξ/l)​B^​(q)\displaystyle(1-\xi/l)q+c\cdot e+(\xi/l)\hat{B}(q)
=\displaystyle= H⁡(q)+c⋅e\displaystyle H(q)+c\cdot e

Step (a)(a) follows from the law invariance of ERM. Then we have

H​q−c⋅e≤H⁡(q−c⋅e)≤H⁡(q+c⋅e)≤H​q+c⋅eHq-c\cdot e\leq H(q-c\cdot e)\leq H(q+c\cdot e)\leq Hq+c\cdot e

∎

Random Noise Analysis

We restate Lemma C.16 in [41] here as Lemma A.2.4, which is useful for proving properties of the random noise.

Lemma A.2.4 (Lemma C.16 in [41]).

Under Assumption 4.4.1:

ℙ[s~i′=s′|𝒢i−1,b~i,ξ~i,ℱi]=p(s~i,a~i,s′),a.s.,\mathbb{P}[\tilde{s}^{\prime}_{i}=s^{\prime}|\mathcal{G}_{i-1},\tilde{b}_{i},\tilde{\xi}_{i},\mathcal{F}_{i}]=p(\tilde{s}_{i},\tilde{a}_{i},s^{\prime}),a.s.,

for each s′∈𝒮s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S} and i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}.

Lemma A.2.5.

The noise ϕ~i\tilde{\phi}_{i} defined in (A.5) satisfies

𝔼⁡[ϕ~i​(s,a,β)|ℱi]=0,∀s∈𝒮,a∈𝒜,β∈ℬ,i∈ℕ\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(s,a,\beta)|\mathcal{F}_{i}]=0,\forall s\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A},\beta\in\mathcal{B},i\in\mathbb{N}

almost surely, where ℱi\mathcal{F}_{i} is defined in (A.7).

Proof.

Let b:=(s,a,β)b:=(s,a,\beta), b~i:=(s~i,a~i,β)\tilde{b}_{i}:=(\tilde{s}_{i},\tilde{a}_{i},\beta) and i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}. We decompose the expectation using the law of total expectation to get

𝔼[ϕ~i(b)∣ℱi]=𝔼[ϕ~i(b)∣ℱi,b~i≠b]⋅ℙ[b~i≠b∣ℱi]+𝔼[ϕ~i(b)∣ℱi,b~i=b]⋅ℙ[b~i=b∣ℱi]\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i}]=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}\neq b]\cdot\mathbb{P}[\tilde{b}_{i}\neq b\mid\mathcal{F}_{i}]+\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b]\cdot\mathbb{P}[\tilde{b}_{i}=b\mid\mathcal{F}_{i}] (A.10)

From the definition in (A.5), we have

𝔼[ϕ~i(b)∣ℱi,b~i≠b]⋅ℙ[b~i≠b∣ℱi]=0\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}\neq b]\cdot\mathbb{P}[\tilde{b}_{i}\neq b\mid\mathcal{F}_{i}]=0

Then

𝔼[ϕ~i(b)∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b] =𝔼[(Hs~′q~i)(b)−(Hq~i)(b)∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(H_{\tilde{s}^{\prime}}\tilde{q}_{i})(b)-(H\tilde{q}_{i})(b)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b]
=ξ⋅𝔼[−(Gs~′q~i)(b)+(Gq~i)(b)∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle=\xi\cdot\mathbb{E}[-(G_{\tilde{s}^{\prime}}\tilde{q}_{i})(b)+(G\tilde{q}_{i})(b)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b]
=ξ⋅𝔼[𝔼[−(Gs~′q~i)(b)∣ℱi,b~i=b,η~i,𝒢i−1]+(Gq~i)(b)∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle=\xi\cdot\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[-(G_{\tilde{s}^{\prime}}\tilde{q}_{i})(b)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b,\tilde{\eta}_{i},\mathcal{G}_{i-1}]+(G\tilde{q}_{i})(b)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b]
=(a)ξ⋅𝔼[𝔼a,s[−(Gs~1q~i)(b)]+(Gq~i)(b)∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(a)}}}{{=}}\xi\cdot\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}^{a,s}[-(G_{\tilde{s}_{1}}\tilde{q}_{i})(b)]+(G\tilde{q}_{i})(b)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b]
=ξ⋅𝔼[−(Gq~i)(b)+(Gq~i)(b)∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle=\xi\cdot\mathbb{E}[-(G\tilde{q}_{i})(b)+(G\tilde{q}_{i})(b)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b]
=0\displaystyle=0

When s~1\tilde{s}_{1} is used in an expectation with subscript, such as 𝔼a,s\mathbb{E}^{a,s}, then it does not represent a sample s~i\tilde{s}_{i} with i=1i=1, but instead it represents the transition from s~0=s\tilde{s}_{0}=s to s~1\tilde{s}_{1} distributed as p(s,a,⋅)p(s,a,\cdot). Step (a) follows the fact the randomness of (Gs~i′​q~i)​(b)(G_{\tilde{s}^{\prime}_{i}}\tilde{q}_{i})(b) only comes from s~i′\tilde{s}^{\prime}_{i} when conditioning on ℱi,b~i=b,η~i\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b,\tilde{\eta}_{i}, and 𝒢i−1\mathcal{G}_{i-1}.

Then, we have

𝔼⁡[ϕ~i​(b)∣ℱi]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i}] =𝔼[ϕ~i(b)∣ℱi,b~i≠b]⋅ℙ[b~i≠b∣ℱi]+𝔼[ϕ~i(b)∣ℱi,b~i=b]⋅ℙ[b~i=b∣ℱi]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}\neq b]\cdot\mathbb{P}[\tilde{b}_{i}\neq b\mid\mathcal{F}_{i}]+\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b]\cdot\mathbb{P}[\tilde{b}_{i}=b\mid\mathcal{F}_{i}]
=0+0⋅ℙ⁡[b~i=b∣ℱi]\displaystyle=0+0\cdot\mathbb{P}[\tilde{b}_{i}=b\mid\mathcal{F}_{i}]
=0\displaystyle=0

∎

Lemma A.2.6.

The noise ϕ~i\tilde{\phi}_{i} defined in (A.5) satisfies

𝔼⁡[(ϕ~i​(s,a,β))2|ℱi]≤A+B​‖q~i‖∞2,∀s∈𝒮,a∈𝒜,β∈ℬ,i∈ℕ\mathbb{E}[(\tilde{\phi}_{i}(s,a,\beta))^{2}|\mathcal{F}_{i}]\leq A+B\|\tilde{q}_{i}\|^{2}_{\infty},\quad\forall s\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A},\beta\in\mathcal{B},i\in\mathbb{N}

almost surely for some A,B∈ℝ+A,B\in\mathbb{R}_{+}, ℱi\mathcal{F}_{i} is defined in (A.7).

Proof.

Let b:=(s,a,β)b:=(s,a,\beta), b~i:=(s~i,a~i,β)\tilde{b}_{i}:=(\tilde{s}_{i},\tilde{a}_{i},\beta) and i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}. We decompose the expectation using the law of total expectation to get

𝔼⁡[ϕ~i​(b)2∣ℱi]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i}] =𝔼[ϕ~i(b)2∣ℱi,b~i≠b]⋅ℙ[b~i≠b∣ℱi]+𝔼[ϕ~i(b)2∣ℱi,b~i=b]⋅ℙ[b~i=b∣ℱi]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}\neq b]\cdot\mathbb{P}[\tilde{b}_{i}\neq b\mid\mathcal{F}_{i}]+\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b]\cdot\mathbb{P}[\tilde{b}_{i}=b\mid\mathcal{F}_{i}]
=𝔼[ϕ~i(b)2∣ℱi,b~i=b]⋅ℙ[b~i=b∣ℱi]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b]\cdot\mathbb{P}[\tilde{b}_{i}=b\mid\mathcal{F}_{i}]

This is because 𝔼[ϕ~i(b)2∣ℱi,b~i≠b]=0\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}\neq b]=0. Let us evaluate 𝔼[ϕ~i(b)2∣ℱi,b~i=b]\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b].

𝔼[ϕ~i(b)2∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b] =𝔼[((Hs~i′q~i)(b)−(Hq~i)(b))2∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\Bigl((H_{\tilde{s}^{\prime}_{i}}\tilde{q}_{i})(b)-(H\tilde{q}_{i})(b)\Bigr)^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b\Bigr]
=𝔼[(−ξ⋅(Gs~i′q~i)(b)+ξ⋅(Gq~i)(b))2∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\Bigl(-\xi\cdot(G_{\tilde{s}^{\prime}_{i}}\tilde{q}_{i})(b)+\xi\cdot(G\tilde{q}_{i})(b)\Bigr)^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b\Bigr]
=ξ2⋅𝔼[𝔼[(−(Gs~i′q~i)(b)+(Gq~i)(b))2∣ℱi,b~i=b,𝒢i−1]∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle=\xi^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}\Biggl[\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\Bigl(-(G_{\tilde{s}^{\prime}_{i}}\tilde{q}_{i})(b)+(G\tilde{q}_{i})(b)\Bigr)^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b,\mathcal{G}_{i-1}\Bigr]\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b\Biggr]

Let us define δi~​(s′,β)\tilde{\delta_{i}}(s^{\prime},\beta) in (A.11).

δi~​(s′,β)=r⁡(s,a,s′)+maxa′∈𝒜⁡q~i​(s′,a′,β)−q~i​(s,a,β)\tilde{\delta_{i}}(s^{\prime},\beta)=r(s,a,s^{\prime})+\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\tilde{q}_{i}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime},\beta)-\tilde{q}_{i}(s,a,\beta) (A.11)
ξ2⋅𝔼[𝔼[(−(Gs~i′q~i)(b)+(Gq~i)(b))2∣ℱi,b~i=b,η~i,𝒢i−1]∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle\xi^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}\Biggl[\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\Bigl(-(G_{\tilde{s}^{\prime}_{i}}\tilde{q}_{i})(b)+(G\tilde{q}_{i})(b)\Bigr)^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b,\tilde{\eta}_{i},\mathcal{G}_{i-1}\Bigr]\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b\Biggr]
=(a)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(a)}}}{{=}} ξ2⋅𝔼[𝔼a,s[((Gs~1q~i)(b)−(Gq~i)(b))2]∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle\xi^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}\Biggl[\mathbb{E}^{a,s}\Bigl[\Bigl((G_{\tilde{s}_{1}}\tilde{q}_{i})(b)-(G\tilde{q}_{i})(b)\Bigr)^{2}\Bigr]\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b\Biggr]
=(b)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(b)}}}{{=}} ξ2⋅𝔼[𝔼a,s[(𝔼[∂ℓβ(δi~(s~1,β))∣s~1]−𝔼a,s[∂ℓβ(δi~(s~1,β))])2]∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle\xi^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}\biggl[\mathbb{E}^{a,s}\Bigl[\Bigl(\mathbb{E}[\partial\ell_{\beta}(\tilde{\delta_{i}}(\tilde{s}_{1},\beta))\mid\tilde{s}_{1}]-\mathbb{E}^{a,s}[\partial\ell_{\beta}(\tilde{\delta_{i}}(\tilde{s}_{1},\beta))]\Bigr)^{2}\Bigr]\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b\biggr]
=(c)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(c)}}}{{=}} ξ2⋅𝔼[(𝔼a,s[(𝔼[∂ℓβ(δi~(s~1,β))∣s~1])2]−(𝔼a,s[∂ℓβ(δi~(s~1,β))])2])∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle\xi^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}\biggl[\Bigl(\mathbb{E}^{a,s}\Bigl[\bigl(\mathbb{E}[\partial\ell_{\beta}(\tilde{\delta_{i}}(\tilde{s}_{1},\beta))\mid\tilde{s}_{1}]\bigr)^{2}\Bigr]-\Bigl(\mathbb{E}^{a,s}[\partial\ell_{\beta}(\tilde{\delta_{i}}(\tilde{s}_{1},\beta))]\Bigr)^{2}\Bigr]\Bigr)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b\biggr]
≤\displaystyle\leq ξ2⋅𝔼[𝔼a,s[(𝔼[∂ℓβ(δi~(s~1,β))∣s~1])2]∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle\xi^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}\biggl[\mathbb{E}^{a,s}\Bigl[\bigl(\mathbb{E}[\partial\ell_{\beta}(\tilde{\delta_{i}}(\tilde{s}_{1},\beta))\mid\tilde{s}_{1}]\bigr)^{2}\Bigr]\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b\biggr]
≤(d)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(d)}}}{{\leq}} ξ2⋅𝔼[maxs′∈𝒮∂ℓβ(δi~(s′,β))2∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle\xi^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}\biggl[\max_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}\partial\ell_{\beta}(\tilde{\delta_{i}}(s^{\prime},\beta))^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b\biggr]
≤(e)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(e)}}}{{\leq}} ξ2⋅𝔼[maxs′∈𝒮(∣∂ℓβ(δi~(s′,β))−∂ℓβ(0)∣)2∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle\xi^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}\biggl[\max_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}(\mid\partial\ell_{\beta}(\tilde{\delta_{i}}(s^{\prime},\beta))-\partial\ell_{\beta}(0)\mid)^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b\biggr]
≤(f)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(f)}}}{{\leq}} ξ2⋅𝔼[maxs′∈𝒮(βeβ​zmin⋅∣δi~(s′,β)∣)2∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle\xi^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}\biggl[\max_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}(\frac{\beta}{e^{\beta z_{\min}}}\cdot\mid\tilde{\delta_{i}}(s^{\prime},\beta)\mid)^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b\biggr]
≤\displaystyle\leq ξ2⋅(βeβ​zmin)2⋅𝔼[maxs′∈𝒮(δi~(s′,β))2∣ℱi,b~i=b]\displaystyle\xi^{2}\cdot(\frac{\beta}{e^{\beta z_{\min}}})^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}\biggl[\max_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}(\tilde{\delta_{i}}(s^{\prime},\beta))^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b\biggr]
≤(g)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{(g)}}}{{\leq}} ξ2⋅(βeβ​zmin)2⋅(2⋅‖r‖∞2+8⋅‖q~i‖∞2)\displaystyle\xi^{2}\cdot(\frac{\beta}{e^{\beta z_{\min}}})^{2}\cdot(2\cdot\|r\|_{\infty}^{2}+8\cdot\|\tilde{q}_{i}\|^{2}_{\infty})

Step (a)(a) follows Lemma A.2.4 given that the randomness of −(Gs~i′​q~i)​(b)+(G​q~i)​(b)-(G_{\tilde{s}^{\prime}_{i}}\tilde{q}_{i})(b)+(G\tilde{q}_{i})(b) only comes from s~i′\tilde{s}^{\prime}_{i} when conditioning on ℱi,b~i=b,η~i\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b,\tilde{\eta}_{i} and 𝒢i−1\mathcal{G}_{i-1}. Step (b)(b) follows by substituting (Gs~i′​q~i)​(b)(G_{\tilde{s}^{\prime}_{i}}\tilde{q}_{i})(b) with (A.2), substituting (G​q~i)​(b)(G\tilde{q}_{i})(b) with (A.3), and replacing by using δ~i\tilde{\delta}_{i} defined in (A.11). The equality in step (c)(c) holds because for a random variable x~=𝔼⁡[∂ℓβ​(δi~​(s~1,β))∣s~1]\tilde{x}=\mathbb{E}[\partial\ell_{\beta}(\tilde{\delta_{i}}(\tilde{s}_{1},\beta))\mid\tilde{s}_{1}], the variance satisfies 𝔼⁡[(x~−𝔼⁡[x~])2]=𝔼⁡[x~2]−(𝔼⁡[x~])2\mathbb{E}[(\tilde{x}-\mathbb{E}[\tilde{x}])^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{x}^{2}]-(\mathbb{E}[\tilde{x}])^{2}. Step (d)(d) upper bounds the expectation by a maximum. Step (e)(e) uses ∂ℓβ​(0)=0\partial\ell_{\beta}(0)=0 from the definition in (4.11). Step (f)(f) uses Lemma 4.4.4 to bound the derivative difference as a function of the step size. Step (g)(g) derives the final upper bound since

‖r‖∞=maxs,s′∈𝒮,a∈𝒜⁡|r⁡(s,a,s′)|,‖q~i‖∞=maxs∈𝒮,a∈𝒜⁡|q~i​(s,a,β)|\|r\|_{\infty}=\max_{s,s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A}}|r(s,a,s^{\prime})|,\quad\|\tilde{q}_{i}\|_{\infty}=\max_{s\in\mathcal{S},a\in\mathcal{A}}|\tilde{q}_{i}(s,a,\beta)|
maxs′∈𝒮⁡δ~i​(s′,β)2\displaystyle\max_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}\tilde{\delta}_{i}(s^{\prime},\beta)^{2} ≤(‖r‖∞+2​‖q~i‖∞)2\displaystyle\leq(\|r\|_{\infty}+2\|\tilde{q}_{i}\|_{\infty})^{2} (A.12)
≤(‖r‖∞+2​‖q~i‖∞)2+(‖r‖∞−2​‖q~i‖∞)2\displaystyle\leq(\|r\|_{\infty}+2\|\tilde{q}_{i}\|_{\infty})^{2}+(\|r\|_{\infty}-2\|\tilde{q}_{i}\|_{\infty})^{2}
=2​‖r‖∞2+8​‖q~i‖∞2\displaystyle=2\|r\|_{\infty}^{2}+8\|\tilde{q}_{i}\|_{\infty}^{2}

Then, we have

𝔼⁡[ϕ~i​(b)2∣ℱi]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i}] =𝔼[ϕ~i(b)2∣ℱi,b~i=b]⋅ℙ[b~i=b∣ℱi]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\phi}_{i}(b)^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i},\tilde{b}_{i}=b]\cdot\mathbb{P}[\tilde{b}_{i}=b\mid\mathcal{F}_{i}]
≤ξ2⋅(βeβ​zmin)2⋅(2⋅‖r‖∞2+8⋅‖q~i‖∞2)\displaystyle\leq\xi^{2}\cdot(\frac{\beta}{e^{\beta z_{\min}}})^{2}\cdot(2\cdot\|r\|_{\infty}^{2}+8\cdot\|\tilde{q}_{i}\|^{2}_{\infty})

Therefore, A=ξ2⋅(βeβ​zmin)2⋅(2⋅‖r‖∞2)A=\xi^{2}\cdot(\frac{\beta}{e^{\beta z_{\min}}})^{2}\cdot(2\cdot\|r\|_{\infty}^{2}) and B=8​ξ2⋅(βeβ​zmin)2B=8\xi^{2}\cdot(\frac{\beta}{e^{\beta z_{\min}}})^{2}. ∎

Now, we are ready to prove Theorem 4.4.2.

Proof.

We verify that the sequence of our qq-learning iterates satisfies the properties in Proposition A.1.3. The step size condition in Theorem 4.4.2 guarantees that we satisfy property (a)(a) in Proposition A.1.3. Lemma A.2.5 and Lemma A.2.6 show that we satisfy property (b) in Proposition A.1.3. Lemma A.2.3 shows that we satisfy property (c)(c) in Proposition A.1.3. ∎
